docs.title: labdex
docs.text:
A small inventory for homelabs that treats zones and names as first-class. Describe networks, hosts, interfaces and services once; labdex checks them against your conventions and generates what the rest of the lab needs (firewall aliases, DNS records, an Ansible inventory, DHCP reservations, login banners) and, through plugins, keeps your firewall, DNS server and monitoring in step with it.

Built with AI, for home labs only

labdex was written largely with an AI coding assistant (Claude), directed and reviewed by a human. It has a test suite and was security-reviewed, but it has not had an independent audit and may contain security problems. Run it in a home lab on a trusted network, behind your own access controls; don't expose it to the internet or use it for production or business infrastructure.

It sits between a spreadsheet and NetBox: one container, SQLite (or PostgreSQL), well under 100 MB of RAM, and a YAML file you can keep in git.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Inventory and IPAM: networks with VLANs, IPv4/IPv6 prefixes and DHCP ranges; hosts with interfaces and services; next free address per network.
  • Zones <AREA>_<TRUST> on every network and host, a zone matrix of who may reach whom, and lint that keeps devices out of zones above their trust level.
  • Naming rules: functional names (srv-vm-dns-01) plus memorable fun names.
  • Plans you approve: anything that changes another system (firewall rules and aliases, DNS records, port forwards, Ansible runs) is planned first, shown as a diff, and applied after the approvals your policy asks for, inside change windows.
  • Plugins: OPNsense, Technitium DNS, Ansible, nmap, VictoriaMetrics/Prometheus, Beszel, Uptime Kuma, Proxmox VE, k3s, Tailscale/Headscale, UniFi, routing (FRR, IOS-XE), certificates, backups. Write your own in Python or Ansible; install signed ones from repositories.
  • Users, roles and history: roles bound to zones, areas, networks or tags; every change recorded with a diff and revertable.

Try it without installing anything in demo mode, or go straight to Install.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • No more InsecureRequestWarning in the log for every request to a device whose certificate isn't checked (a self-signed firewall, controller or hypervisor, with "verify TLS" off): that's a setting you chose, not a problem to report again and again.

docs.title: labdex moved to labdex-app
docs.text:
• labdex, its Marketplace and the official plugins now live in the GitHub organization labdex-app. Old links redirect.
  • The image is now ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex. Change it in your compose file once: ghcr.io/reykimedev/labdex stays at 1.24.0 and gets no more updates.
  • The official Marketplace is at https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex-plugins/index.json; labdex moves its official repository there by itself. The docs are at https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex/. An instance that still has the old project address (Settings › General) gets the new one; one you set yourself stays.

docs.title: Faster
docs.text: • The services list is about 9× faster with 1000 hosts: permission checks no longer build each host's full record (the same for DNS, racks, Discovery and the audit log).

docs.title: Plugins come from the Marketplace only
docs.text:
• No plugin ships with labdex any more, the official ones included: the image and the wheel are labdex alone, and every plugin is installed from Plugins › Marketplace (or uploaded), downloaded and signature-checked like any other.
  • Backups are part of labdex: the backup plugin moved into the core, so every instance has its daily backup from the first start, as before. The Marketplace no longer offers it.
  • Upgrading from 1.24.0: labdex installs the official plugins you had (installed, or with an instance) from the official Marketplace by itself, at their held version if you held one, a few seconds after the start. Offline, it tries again every 15 minutes, and the Plugins page lists what's missing with an Install them now button; instances keep their settings and history meanwhile. A plugin you uninstall isn't put back.
  • The demo only has the plugins of its own image (the demo lab and backups).
  • For development: the official plugins are git submodules in plugins/ (not in the package); LABDEX_DEV_PLUGINS loads such checkouts, the tests set it.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• labdex 1.24.0 didn't start when the official Marketplace had been added by hand before (under its name or address): it now takes that entry over. A problem setting up the official repository can no longer stop labdex from starting.
  • The release's source archive is labdex alone (it included the plugins).

docs.title: Licence
docs.text: • labdex is now under the GNU AGPL-3.0 (was MIT), with a plugin exception: free to use and change, but a changed labdex, also one run as a service, has to stay open source and keep the credit to the original (see NOTICE). Plugins can use any licence; the official ones are AGPL-3.0 too. Earlier releases stay MIT.

docs.title: Patch panels and cable traces
docs.text:
• An interface can pass through to another port of the same host: a patch panel's front port and its rear port (set on one side, both get it). Several adds a whole panel at once, every port with its rear port.
  • Trace follows a cable end to end through any number of patch panels, with each cable's label, colour and length: on a host's ports, on the Cables page and on a topology cable.

docs.title: Where is this MAC?
docs.text:
• Discovery › Where is… finds the switch port behind a MAC, an IP address or a host, from the switches' forwarding tables; the likely port is pinned (an uplink to another switch isn't). Typing a MAC or an address in the search offers it too, and a host's Network tab shows the port next to each interface that has no cable on record.
  • SNMP neighbours 1.1 reads BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB (per VLAN); UniFi 2.2 reports every client's switch port (wired) or access point (Wi-Fi). Publish both from their repositories.
  • For plugin authors: ctx.discovery.record_macs(source, entries).

docs.title: Sign in with OpenID Connect
docs.text: • Authentik, Keycloak, Authelia, Pocket ID, Zitadel …: authorization code flow with PKCE, accounts created at the first sign-in (or only existing ones), groups from the provider matched to labdex groups, administrators by group, the password form optional. Configured through LABDEX_OIDC_*; Settings › Users shows the setup and the redirect URI.

docs.title: The top bar
docs.text: • Help, the project's page, About, Settings and your account sit in a bar at the top; the sidebar lost its duplicate Collapse, Admin and avatar. Admin is now Settings. A Help page has the docs, issues, security reports, the keyboard and the details for a bug report.

docs.title: Release check
docs.text: • The update check works with GitHub, GitLab and Gitea/Forgejo (Codeberg …) from the project's address (Settings › General; default github.com/reykimedev/labdex), says why a check failed, and tries again after ten minutes instead of six hours.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
• Pushes get a quick lint; the full tests run on pull requests.
  • Release images are built on native amd64 and arm64 runners in parallel (no emulation) and joined into one multi-arch image; each architecture keeps its own build cache.
  • Dependabot keeps GitHub Actions, npm, Python, the base image and the plugin submodules up to date, as weekly pull requests.

docs.title: Faster image builds
docs.text:
• The UI is built once on the runner's own platform instead of again under arm64 emulation; system packages and Python dependencies are a layer that only changes with pyproject.toml; layers are cached in the registry (:buildcache) between releases.
  • CI uses actions that run on Node 24.

docs.title: Plugin versions and updates
docs.text:
• A plugin's details in the Marketplace show what's new since your version and every version its repository offers, with release notes and dates. Install any of them, newer or older.
  • Switch back: an update keeps the version it replaced, so going back is one click (and works offline). Going forward again works the same way.
  • Stay on a version: a held plugin gets no update offers and never updates by itself.
  • Withdrawn versions: publishers can withdraw a version with a reason. Whoever has it is warned in the Marketplace and by notification, and updates skip it.
  • Update checks every six hours (Admin › Plugins › Updates): Tell me (the default) sends a notification per new version once; Install official updates installs updates signed with the labdex project key by themselves, into History; Off. New notification events: plugins.update, plugins.updated, plugins.update_failed, plugins.withdrawn.
  • Official plugins have a CHANGELOG, shown in the Marketplace.

docs.title: Plugins in their own repositories
docs.text:
• Every plugin that ships with labdex moves to a repository of its own (labdex-plugin-<id>), included in labdex as a git submodule. Tagging a version there signs it and attaches it to a GitHub release.
  • The official Marketplace is its own repository, labdex-plugins: it lists the plugin repositories, checks every release's signature and publishes a signed index at reykimedev.github.io/labdex-plugins, which labdex trusts out of the box.
  • For publishers: labdex plugin build-index (a Marketplace from plugin repositories), labdex plugin yank (withdraw a version), labdex plugin fetch-repo (keep older versions when rebuilding a repository), tools/plugin_repo/make_plugin_repo.py (start a plugin repository with its release workflow). An index can now list several versions of a plugin and point at archives anywhere.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
• labdex and every plugin are released by publishing a GitHub release (tag v<version>); the workflow checks the tag against the code with a clear message, builds, signs and attaches everything to that release.
  • A release's description gets that version's CHANGELOG section (below anything written by hand), and CHANGELOG.md is attached. The source archive includes the plugins.
  • Plugin repositories: .releaseignore keeps files out of the release zip (labdex plugin prune); the Marketplace finds new labdex-plugin-* repositories by itself and checks for new releases every hour.

docs.title: Also
docs.text:
• README, docs and the About page say plainly that labdex was built with AI and is meant for home labs only.
  • Links point at the real addresses (github.com/reykimedev/labdex, its Pages and ghcr).

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
• Cables are drawn in their own colour. Switch to colouring by speed on the legend (remembered in your browser and in saved views); thicker is still faster. White and black cables get a thin edge so they show on both themes.
  • A host's fun name is a label of its own above the host, in bold; the hostname sits below in mono, quieter. Drag the fun name wherever it reads best: it stays there (shared, with the layout) and moves with the host.
  • Port names are small tags further out along the cable, clear of the host and its name.
  • Snap to grid works: the dots were drawn half a step off the points things snap to. The dots are a little easier to see too.
  • Hypervisor boxes leave room for their guests' names.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
• Network › Policy has a second tab, On the firewalls: every firewall that enforces the matrix shows its pending rule changes, the rules no policy explains and which zones labdex manages, with Sync policy rules right there. It replaces the OPNsense instance's Firewall policy tab (old links land on the new tab).
  • For plugin authors: place: policy on a page (with an action) puts it there.
  • OPNsense plugin 1.3.

docs.title: Plugin Marketplace
docs.text:
• Plugins › Marketplace: every plugin that ships with labdex and everything your repositories offer, in one place: search, categories, Not installed / Installed / Updates, and a details view with what each plugin brings (settings, actions, pages, where it comes from). Installing a plugin that ships with labdex is one click and downloads nothing; a download from a repository is signature-checked and confirmed as before.
  • Not everything is installed by default. A new labdex starts with Backup, File exports, Ansible runner and nmap. An upgrade keeps those plus every plugin you have an instance of, so nothing you use goes away.
  • Uninstall a plugin that ships with labdex from the Marketplace (refused while it has instances). It stays part of labdex; install it again any time.
  • A plugin's page says when it isn't installed, with an Install button.
  • Admin › Plugins keeps upload, repositories and signing keys; the repository list now sends you to the Marketplace to install.
  • The Marketplace view is open to everyone who can see integrations; installing needs an administrator, as before.
  • An inventory import keeps the instance's plugin choices (and the official-repository setting) instead of resetting them.

docs.title: Cables the switches see
docs.text:
• Inventory › Cables › Seen by switches: cables switches report that aren't on record yet (tick and add, or ignore for good), ports where a switch sees something else than the record (keep it, or use what's seen), and neighbours labdex doesn't know (add them as hosts, prefilled). A cable both ends report shows once; adding one goes through the host's normal checks and into History.
  • New plugin SNMP neighbours: reads LLDP-MIB and CISCO-CDP-MIB over SNMP v2c or v3 (SHA, SHA-256, SHA-512, MD5; AES-128), reports whether each switch answers and shows its neighbours on the host. It starts with hosts tagged snmp. Its SNMP client is labdex's own (no new dependency) and is tested against net-snmp.
  • UniFi 2.1: signed in with a local account it also reads LLDP tables, device uplinks and the switch port of every wired client.
  • Ends are matched to hosts by any name labdex knows, an interface's MAC, or an address; port names match whatever their case, and the cable uses the host's own spelling.

docs.title: For plugin authors
docs.text:
• ctx.discovery.record_links(source, links) reports what a device sees on its ports.
  • applies_to in a manifest: what a new instance applies to (the default stays *).
A UI pass: every page looked at in light, dark and on a phone.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A network's page showed its id (GPUUVNFHZD) as the title instead of its name.
  • A host's Plugins tab was blank when no plugin works per host; it says so now.
  • A host's DNS records ran off the screen on a phone.
  • The Overview dashboard had empty stretches and cut off Last changes; its default layout is tighter (updated for everyone who never changed it).
  • A plugin page's title (and any name set in mono) was smaller than every other title.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• The last radio buttons and tick lists are gone: the home zone (follow the primary interface / choose), a secret's source (own value / from the vault) and a plugin per host (follow / always on / off) are segmented controls; network pickers in plugin settings are chips; yes/no columns in plugin tables are switches. Tick boxes stay only where you pick rows to act on.
  • One rule for buttons: one primary button per screen (what the page creates); adding inside a section is a normal button.
  • Plugin actions all look alike, with an icon for plans first or runs right away (purple and grey ones read as enabled and disabled).
  • A colour picker's "any colour" button is a rainbow swatch; a picked custom colour gets a swatch of its own.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
• Host: the rack on its own line with unit and side below; on a phone the hostname parts sit two by two; the home zone picker isn't squeezed.
  • Network: a prefix's gateway and DHCP range on one line, its description below.
  • Hosts on a phone: function (and a status other than active) under the name, so the name column has room.
  • Topology: the toolbar fits one line; the speed legend sits on the map; PNG, SVG and Arrange again are under ⋯.
  • Zones: rank and counts line up whether or not a zone can be deleted.
  • Discovery: a count of zero is no longer red.
  • Links in tables are coloured and underlined only on hover, everywhere.
  • Backup plugin 1.2: the folder or the S3 settings, whichever Where to says.

docs.title: One place for secrets
docs.text:
• The vault holds every shared secret. Admin › Secrets is gone: its secrets move into the vault as global/<name> (field value) the first time an administrator sets the vault up or unseals it, written to History. Nothing that pointed at them breaks: a bare name keeps meaning vault:global/<name>#value, and /api/secrets works on those entries.
  • Plugins point at vault fields: a secret setting offers from the vault with every field you may use (fw/opnsense#key). Ansible variables too: {$secret: vault:fw/opnsense#key}. The value is read when the job runs.
  • Pointing at a secret needs secret:apply on it (the right to reveal it), since it hands the secret to a plugin or to Ansible. References someone else saved stay when you edit. New endpoint /api/vault/refs lists what you may point at.
  • An entry shows who uses it; it can't be deleted while anything does, and renaming it takes the references along.
  • While the vault is sealed, jobs that need a secret fail and say why.
  • Lint reports variables that point at a vault field that doesn't exist.
  • The public demo can't set up or change the vault.

docs.title: Cables
docs.text:
• A cable has a label (what's printed on it), a length in metres and a jacket colour, on every cable dialog. Next free continues the lab's own numbering (C-0042 → C-0043); a label belongs to one cable only.
  • Inventory › Cables: every cable in one list, searchable, editable, with printable labels: two per cable, each naming this end and the other one.
  • Front panel: a host with four ports or more shows them on its Dashboard and Network tab like the front of a switch (odd on top, cages apart), lit in the cable's speed colour. Point at a port for where it goes, click it for its cable.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
• Saved views: picture, zone, hidden networks, options and zoom under a name, for everyone, opened from the list or by link.
  • PNG and SVG download of the whole picture.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • A cable inside one host survives a YAML import.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
• Networks (L3): chips above the map hide and show single networks; a hidden network takes its lines along, and hosts left with none.
  • Hosts show their fun name with the hostname below. A host can have its own colour on the map (Overview › Colour on the map); otherwise its zone's.
  • Grid: a dot grid that pans and zooms with the map; what you drop snaps to it (a box keeps its guests' arrangement).
  • VIPs are joined to the hosts that hold them in the L3 view, and left out of the physical one.
  • Port names at the ends of cables (they fade out when you zoom far out). Click a line for its two ends and details; a cable's medium, speed and notes can be changed or the cable removed right there.
  • Point at a host for a summary card: names, function, zone, status, address.
  • Guests on their hypervisor: a guest interface that doesn't say what it sits on is joined to the hypervisor's bridge in the same network, drawn fainter as a guess.
  • Cables inside one host: draw them on the map (click the same host twice) or add them on its Network tab (the host itself is offered as the far end). They show as a loop.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
• Physical and virtual interfaces are listed apart: ports first, then bonds, bridges, VLANs, tunnels and loopbacks under what they sit on.
  • A physical port has a connector (RJ45, SFP, SFP+, SFP28, QSFP+, QSFP28, QSFP-DD …) and a speed; picking a connector offers its usual speed.
  • Several: add many interfaces at once from a pattern: eth[0-3], 1/0/[1-48], swp[1-4]s[0-3], Gi1/0/[01-24].

docs.title: And
docs.text:
• Sidebar sections open and close with a short slide; closed ones are out of the tab order.
  • Features from a dotted path: making test.test.test makes test and test.test as well when they're missing (UI, API and YAML import), each with its own history entry.

docs.title: Vault
docs.text:
• Inventory › Vault: labdex's own store for root passwords, IPMI logins, Wi-Fi keys and recovery codes. Entries have a path (hosts/srv-pm-pve-01/root), an optional host, a description and named fields; a button makes a strong password in the browser.
  • Sealed start: the vault is encrypted with a passphrase labdex never stores. After every start an administrator unseals it; until then names show and values don't. Five wrong passphrases a minute, then a pause. Seal it by hand any time; change the passphrase without touching the entries.
  • Envelope encryption: scrypt and AES-256-GCM for the master key, a fresh data key per version, each ciphertext bound to its entry and version. A database copy or a backup alone opens nothing.
  • Values show one field at a time, for 30 seconds, or are copied without showing; each reveal is in History. The browser asks for your password again before the first reveal and every 5 minutes after.
  • Every change is a new version; the last 10 are kept and can be revealed.
  • Hosts have a Secrets tab with their entries and + Secret for this host; the host's rights apply to them and they follow the host through renames and YAML imports.
  • New permission type secret and the built-in role secret-keeper. A * role or grant covers only viewing secrets: revealing (secret:apply) and changing (secret:edit) are always given by name. Path scopes work: name:wifi/*.
  • Docs: The vault under Concepts, with how it's built.

docs.title: Racks
docs.text:
• Inventory › Racks: every rack as an elevation, front and rear side by side, grouped by site. Click a free unit to put a host there; a host's ⋯ moves it or takes it out. Devices on the front and the rear can share a unit; full-depth ones take both sides. Overlaps are refused with what's in the way.
  • What isn't a host goes in too: patch panels, cable management, blank panels, shelves, PDUs, each with a label and a description.
  • A host has a Size in units (U, HE) of its own, set on its Overview whether or not it's in a rack; putting it in a rack uses it. Its rack, unit and side are there too; the Dashboard tab shows where it sits and links to its rack.
  • Racks are part of the YAML export and import; renaming a rack keeps its hosts.
A review release: tooling, dead code, fixes.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• ESLint (JavaScript and Vue rules) runs with npm run lint and in CI; ruff checks more (pycodestyle, bugbear, pyupgrade, comprehensions). Everything they found is fixed.
  • Forms that edit an object handed to them (service, prefixes, plugin settings) use v-model instead of changing their props.
  • Dead code removed: an unused ARP reader, YAML dumper, trust-level defaults from before zones, unused helpers and exports, a filter function and variables left over in views.
  • The host's dashboard is its own component; shared styles (.g2, .g3, .ell, .hide-m) live once in the stylesheet instead of being copied into views.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Reloading a page several times quickly could leave live updates refused for a while ("too many open event streams"); a new stream now replaces the oldest of yours.
  • Tables inside cards no longer break words letter by letter (the aliases' type column).
  • "Not on a phone" hints were shown on phones: the class only worked in the sidebar.
  • Dashboard links refuse backslashes and line breaks too (/\\host is //host to a browser).
  • The changelog renderer escapes quotes in links.
  • The docs named a host status retired; it's legacy.

docs.title: Small things
docs.text:
• History hides sign-ins unless you tick Sign-ins too, and filters by more object types (zones, areas, tags, features, the zone policy).
  • The aliases table names its last column (Source).

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
• The start page is a dashboard of cards on a 12-column grid. Edit moves cards (drag the handle, or arrow keys), resizes them (the corner, or Shift + arrows), removes and adds them; Done saves. Cards: the numbers, approvals, failing and running jobs, last changes, coming up, hosts per zone, every plugin widget or a single one, your links, the inventory's services with their status (by tag, zone or category), and notes.
  • More dashboards: your own (only you see them) and shared ones (administrators). A new one can start as a page of links: service links, your own links and a note.
  • Link cards only take http(s) addresses or labdex pages; the server refuses anything else, the dialog says so before.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Rows in lists of links (dashboard cards) aren't underlined like links inside a sentence.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
• A host opens on its new Dashboard: status and monitors, addresses, zone, hypervisor, guests and cables, links to its services, and the plugin widgets (they moved here from Overview). The form is under Overview.
  • Addresses per family in the interface dialog, like a network's prefixes: IPv4 address and more IPv4 addresses; IPv6 interface ID or address and more IPv6 addresses. The topology's network view shows the extra addresses too.

docs.title: Stable addresses
docs.text:
• Hosts, networks and zones have a short id that never changes, and pages use it in the address bar (/hosts/7k2m9x4qa1): bookmarks and shared links survive renames. Links by name keep working. The API takes the id wherever it takes a name.
  • Zones have a page: networks, hosts at home there, and what the policy lets in and out. A renamed zone (or a zone whose area is renamed) keeps its id.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • An unsaved draft no longer hides the whole host or network page until you choose Restore or Discard; the page shows below the offer.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
• Two views: Physical (cables, hypervisors with their guests) and Networks (L3 / VLANs): networks as nodes, every host joined to the networks it has an address in; routers and other multi-homed hosts are diamonds. Each view keeps its own shared arrangement.
  • Hosts show their icon. Cables are coloured by speed and thicker when faster, with a legend of the speeds on the map; Wi-Fi links are dotted.
  • Draw cables on the map: Cable, click both ends, pick each side's interface from a list (or name an unnamed one, or add a new port to the host). Saved on both hosts with history; a cable is removed from a host's side panel.

docs.title: Sidebar and forms
docs.text:
• One section open at a time; the section titles are as large as the entries. Detail pages mark their list (a host marks Hosts). Collapse at the bottom and Ctrl B shrink and expand the sidebar.
  • Plugins no longer add sidebar entries: their pages are tabs on the integration. Old links keep working.
  • On/off settings are switches; lists you pick several from keep tick boxes.
  • Cable speeds are offered as a list (100M … 100G) and shown as a colour on the host's Network tab. VIP membership there is a section like interfaces and cables, with space between them.
  • New hosts start as active.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text: • Zone codes are names: type Trusted clients and the zone becomes DC_TRUSTED_CLIENTS. Areas take up to 16 letters or digits, zones up to 48 characters.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text: • nmap also checks the port of every declared TCP service on its host, even outside its port list. Not answering now means a scan looked at that port and found it closed; a port nobody scanned shows not scanned instead of being reported down (and isn't listed as missing).

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: • labdex versions are now MAJOR.MINOR.SUB, and MAJOR.MINOR.SUB-N for the N-th hotfix of a release (bug fixes only; 1.9.0-1 comes after 1.9.0, the next release is 1.10.0). tools/bump.py writes a new version everywhere; the image of a hotfix also moves the tags of its release (1.9.0, 1.9, 1, latest).

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
• Hosts has three tabs: Physical, Virtual (guests of another host, VMs and containers) and VIPs. Host on the Virtual tab starts a guest.
  • The hosts search takes terms: tag:, zone:, status:, cat:, on: (guests of a host) and net:, combined with plain words; several tag: terms must all match. A tag chip in the list adds its term.
  • Group by tag, zone, runs on, category or status, with a heading and count per group.
  • The search box (Ctrl K) offers Hosts tagged … for tag:x or a word that is a tag.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: • The map's arrangement is shared: everyone sees the same positions, and people who may edit hosts move them for all. The hint says who arranged it last; Arrange again starts over for everyone (after asking).

docs.title: Drafts
docs.text: • Host and network forms keep what you type as a draft in this browser for two weeks. Coming back offers it again (Restore them / Discard); Save still applies, and clears the draft.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• UniFi 2.0 signs in the way your setup allows: a local username and password on UniFi OS Server or a UniFi OS console, a username and password on the Network application on its own, a console API key, or a Site Manager API key from unifi.ui.com (every console the key sees, read through the cloud connector; devices still come from Site Manager when the connector can't reach a console). Accounts with two-factor sign-in get a clear message; labdex signs out after every run.
  • Proxmox: Check drift puts guests the inventory doesn't have into Discovery, with address, name and MAC, ready to adopt.
  • Plugin settings can depend on another one (when: {auth: [password]}): the form shows only what applies, and hidden settings are neither required nor lost.

docs.title: Light theme
docs.text: • A light theme next to the dark one: Auto (follows the system), Light or Dark in the menu under your name, or light / dark in the search box. Kept in this browser and applied before the page draws, so it never flashes. Zone and tag colours are darkened in the light theme so they stay readable; the topology redraws in the theme's colours.

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
• No page scrolls sideways any more at phone width: long words and URLs (error messages, for one) wrap, and grids no longer grow past the screen (the Dashboard was 1844 px wide).
  • The hosts list keeps name, function, zone and status on a phone; addresses, links and monitoring columns come back on a wider screen.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• An automated WCAG 2.1 AA check (axe) of 19 pages in both themes finds nothing: faint text, button text and zone chips meet 4.5:1 contrast; links inside sentences are underlined; the policy matrix scrolls with the keyboard; the address grid has the right role.
  • Rows you click to open something (hosts, networks, jobs, history, …) are reachable with Tab and open with Enter. Dialogs keep Tab inside them. "Skip to the page" jumps past the sidebar. Tabs say which one is current. Inputs show a focus ring.
  • The ✕ on fun name, VIP member and feature chips is a real button.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: • Network › Topology draws the lab: a host that others run on is a box with its guests inside and its own interfaces (bridges, bonds, ports) joined the way they're stacked; cables join ports; internal links run from a guest to the bridge it sits on. Filter by zone, find a host or address, click for its links, double-click to open it. Drag to arrange: kept in your browser. New endpoint: GET /api/topology.

docs.title: Internal cables
docs.text: • A cable can be internal: between a guest and the host it runs on (or two guests of one host), typically the guest's NIC on the hypervisor's bridge. The cable dialog offers only those hosts and suggests the other side's interfaces. A bridge holds any number of internal links (a physical port still holds one cable).

docs.title: Address map
docs.text: • A network's Address map tab: every address of its IPv4 prefix, a /24 at a time, as in use, gateway, DHCP pool, seen (by Discovery, not in labdex), conflict (two hosts, or Discovery saw another MAC) or free. Click a free one to make a host with it, a seen one to add it. New endpoint: GET /api/networks/<name>/map.

docs.title: Plans
docs.text: • The job page groups changes by kind and shows, for an update, only the fields that change. Changes can be unticked before approving: the rest is applied, the log says who left out what (skip on POST /api/jobs/<id>/approve). Unticked changes stay unticked when a plan is made again with the same changes.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • A host or network page counted as changed while it was still loading, so leaving it right away asked about unsaved changes (and the button said "Save changes").

docs.title: Search and go
docs.text:
• Ctrl/⌘ K (or / outside a text field) opens one search box: hosts by name, fun name, function, tag, address or MAC (typed any way); networks by name, VLAN or an address inside them; services; aliases by name or firewall id; integrations, and the actions you may run there (Enter starts one and opens the job); pages; New host, VIP or network. Only what you may see. A Search button sits at the top of the sidebar.
  • New endpoint: GET /api/search?q=.

docs.title: Many hosts at once
docs.text: • Tick hosts on the list (Shift-click for a range, the header box for all shown) and change status, runs on, tags (add and remove) or an integration (on, off, as its selectors say) for all of them, or delete them. All or nothing; each host gets its own history entry with the same summary. New endpoint: POST /api/hosts/bulk.

docs.title: Keeping your place
docs.text:
• Back and forward return to the scroll position you left. DNS, Discovery and History are kept alive like the other lists (they refresh in the background when shown again).
  • Ctrl/⌘ S saves a host or network; leaving one with unsaved changes asks first, also when closing the tab.
  • A search link to an alias opens the Aliases page filtered to it.

docs.title: Smaller things
docs.text:
• One heading on the Zones page ("Areas and zones").
  • Long notification messages are cut to two lines with "show all".
  • Empty Networks, Services and DNS pages say what to do next.
  • Docs: "Working fast" (shortcuts, search, bulk changes).

docs.title: Isolated plugins
docs.text:
• Community and unsigned plugins no longer run inside labdex. Each call (action, plan, apply, export, page, widget, endpoint, test) runs in a process of its own with an empty environment, which locks itself with Landlock before the plugin is loaded: it can read Python and the plugin's own folder, and write only to a data folder of its own and a temporary folder. It can't open labdex's database or secret.key, other plugins' folders, or labdex's memory and environment, and can't signal labdex.
  • The plugin API reaches labdex over a pipe and answers for that instance only: its own settings and host settings, the inventory, state, host status, notifications and discovery records. Anything else is refused.
  • Their Ansible playbooks (in code or manifest-only actions) run inside the same lock; global secrets aren't filled in for them.
  • labdex's own process is non-dumpable, so no plugin of the same user can read its memory, isolated or not.
  • LABDEX_PLUGIN_SANDBOX: on (default), strict (refuse isolated plugins without Landlock), off (run them inside labdex, as before). The Plugins page shows which plugins run isolated and how isolated they are on this machine; the install dialog says what an unsigned plugin will be able to reach.
  • Official and built-in plugins run inside labdex as before.

docs.title: Plugin API
docs.text:
• ctx.data_dir can also be called (data_dir(), as the reference always said).
  • Ansible runs with a local connection keep their temporary files in the run's folder.

docs.title: Proxmox: creating guests
docs.text:
• Plan a VM or container in the inventory (a planned host with its address, on a Proxmox node) and labdex creates it in Proxmox, as a plan you approve: Create planned guests for all of them, Create this guest on one host. Off until "Create guests" is turned on in the instance.
  • Containers come from an LXC template, VMs are cloned from a cloud-init template. Network, VLAN tag, static address and gateway (or DHCP), IPv6 (static or SLAAC), SSH keys, DNS server and search domain come from the inventory and the instance; cores, memory, disk, storage and template per host override the instance's defaults.
  • A MAC the inventory lacks is generated with Proxmox's prefix, the same in every plan, and written back to the host. The host is linked to its guest and set active once it runs. A guest that was created but failed a later step is still linked (and the host set offline), so it's never created twice.
  • Nothing is ever deleted or changed in Proxmox after creation.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Proxmox: saving a host's Proxmox settings without a guest id stored id 0, which counted as linked to a guest.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
• Every plugin labdex ships is now an official plugin: Ansible, Backup, Certificates, Docker, File exports, k3s, MOTD, nmap, OPNsense, Prometheus SD, Proxmox, Routing, Tailscale, Technitium, Traefik, VictoriaMetrics and YAML mirror join Beszel, Uptime Kuma and UniFi. They still work from the first start, and now get fixes from the official repository between labdex releases. Plugin ids are unchanged, so integrations, settings and history carry over. Only the demo lab stays built in.
  • Each states the labdex versions it works with (>=1.3,<2).
  • Plugins page: a shipped plugin has no Remove button; an installed update of one has "Remove update", which goes back to the shipped version.
  • Only an update signed with the labdex project key can take a shipped plugin's place, at install and when loading: an unsigned or community copy with the same id is refused (labdex keeps the shipped one). Before, ticking "I trust its author" let an unsigned copy stand in for Beszel, Uptime Kuma or UniFi.
  • labdex.discovery.network_of (the network an address belongs to) is public; the old _network_of name still works.
A UI overhaul: one look across every page, fewer things on screen at once, and forms in dialogs instead of inline.

docs.title: Look
docs.text:
• IBM Plex Sans and Mono, a calmer dark palette, one control radius and one box radius, sentence-case headings and labels everywhere (no more all-caps table heads, tile and widget labels), and line icons (Lucide) for actions instead of "Edit", "✕" and "+ …".
  • Lists of things (interfaces, cables, services, zones, tags, hostname parts, fun name pools) are rows with a title, a muted detail line and icon actions on the right.
  • Filters are compact "Label: value" selects on every page (Hosts, Aliases, Services, Discovery, DNS, Lint, History, Plugins) instead of rows of chips.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: • The sidebar is grouped into Inventory, Network, Automation and Audit, each collapsible; the group of the current page opens by itself, and a collapsed group shows its badge. The zone tree is its own collapsible section. What's open is remembered.

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text:
• Create and edit happen in dialogs (Esc or a click outside closes them): areas and zones, aliases, tags, hostname parts, fun name pools, policy cells, job templates, approval policies and change windows, notification channels, users, groups, roles, role bindings, object grants, secrets, plugin instances and author keys.
  • Every "are you sure?" is a labdex dialog that says what happens, not the browser's.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
• The Network tab is a list of interfaces as a tree (bond → bridge → ports), each with its zone, addresses, MAC, cable and what Discovery saw; editing one opens a dialog with next-free buttons, extra addresses and per-prefix IPv6. Cables are their own list.
  • The Services tab lists services and host rules; a service is edited in a dialog with allow-from as chips with suggestions.
  • The hosts list shows at most three addresses ("N more").

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: • Tag colours show everywhere a tag does: the hosts list, the host form's tag input and the tag list; the tag dialog has the same colour swatches as zones.

docs.title: Traefik
docs.text: • New built-in plugin (read-only, Traefik v2/v3 API, optional basic auth). "Import services from routers" plans a service per HTTP router with a Host rule: on the host its backend points at, else on the Traefik host (port 443/80). The router's host name is the service's link; path prefixes and TLS (router TLS or a websecure entry point) carry over. Filters for entry points and providers; a Routers page and a dashboard widget.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: • New built-in plugin (read-only Engine API, best behind a socket proxy; optional bearer token). "Import containers" plans a host per container (srv-ct-<service>-NN, fun name = container name, runs on the Docker host, in its zone; an interface where the container has an address in an inventory network), and services: published ports on the Docker host, Traefik router labels with their host names. Existing hosts are linked by name; nothing is removed. "Read container state" reports running/stopped as host status. Options: services only (no container hosts), stopped containers, ignore patterns, category. A Containers page and a dashboard widget.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A service's DNS name can be a full name ending in a dot (grafana.example.com.): the link uses it as is, and it gets a CNAME only when it lies in a zone labdex writes.
  • Plugins share labdex.plugins.servicesync to plan and apply services found elsewhere: matched by DNS name, then port, then name; only adds and fills in, never removes.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Plugin HTTP clients took any path starting with "http" (like Traefik's http/routers) for a full URL.
labdex is stable: within 1.x the plugin API, the REST API, the inventory YAML and the backup format only grow, and every 1.x starts on a database from any earlier release without a manual step.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
• Bundled official plugins: Beszel, Uptime Kuma and UniFi ship with labdex as official plugins that update on their own. When the official repository has a newer version, the marketplace offers it; the update stands in for the bundled copy, a broken update never does, and removing the update brings the bundled version back.
  • The official repository is there out of the box (removing it is respected), built from backend/labdex/official_plugins and signed with the project key by the docs workflow. LABDEX_OFFICIAL_INDEX points elsewhere or turns it off.
  • The plugin API reference (docs/develop/plugin-api.md) lists what stays stable; plugins name the versions they work with, e.g. labdex: ">=1.0,<2".

docs.title: Docs, releases
docs.text:
• A docs site (MkDocs Material, docs/), published with the official repository to GitHub Pages by docs.yml.
  • Releases: multi-arch images signed with cosign (keyless) with an SPDX SBOM attestation; a GitHub release with the source archive, wheel, sdist, SBOMs, a cosign bundle per file and signed checksums. How to verify: docs → Security.

docs.title: Security review
docs.text:
• Sign-in throttling counts the real client behind a trusted proxy (one client can't lock a user out for everyone behind it) and also limits failures per user overall; the failure table can't grow without bound. History records the client's address.
  • Event streams check every 15 seconds that the user is still active, the session's password unchanged and the API token valid, and a user can hold at most 8 at once.
  • Plugin archives are measured while unpacking (a zip can't lie its way past the size limit); restoring a backup caps the unpacked size.
  • Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, and HSTS when cookies are secure.
  • The review itself: docs/operate/security-review.md.

docs.title: Upgrades
docs.text: • The 1.0 gate is a test: a database with the 0.5.0 schema (the example lab, trust levels, an admin) starts on 1.0, is migrated, and answers every page; nothing on the firewall is renamed (tests/test_upgrade_gate.py).

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
• Alias uids: aliases are called ldx_ and 8 hex digits on the firewall (stable, from the labdex name); the full name stays in the description. New instances use uids; an instance that already has an inventory keeps readable ids until you switch under Admin → Conventions → Firewall ids. Switching renames labdex's aliases on the firewall: sync aliases, then rules; your own rules that use the old names need updating (the policy page lists them).
  • The Aliases page shows the labdex name and the firewall id in their own columns and pages through 50 at a time.
  • Import the firewall's aliases (OPNsense action, optionally limited by name patterns): your own aliases become custom aliases in labdex under their names on the firewall, so nothing is renamed; members that name other aliases become alias references. labdex's and OPNsense's built-in aliases, unsupported types (GeoIP, …) and ones labdex already has are skipped. Turn on "take over" to let labdex manage them.
  • Allow from picks from zones, areas, networks (with their prefixes), prefixes, custom and generated aliases as you type; addresses and CIDRs are fine too, unknown sources are marked.
  • Firewall rules for the whole host (Services tab): allow from a zone, area, network, alias, address or any, or allow to one, on ports (any, port aliases, tcp/443). "Sync policy rules" turns each into pass rules ([host:…], category automation:labdex). YAML: host rules.

docs.title: DNS overview
docs.text: • New DNS page: every record labdex generates (name, type, value, zone, host), and per DNS server (Technitium) every record in the zones it reads, each marked in sync, missing (the next sync creates it), stale (labdex made it, the next sync deletes it) or unmanaged. Filter by status and zone, search, 50 per page. Records of hosts you can't see are left out. API: GET /api/dns; DNS plugins provide dns and a server_records() method.

docs.title: Discovery output
docs.text: • nmap's progress goes into the job log as it scans: each open port as it's found, "x% done" every 15 seconds, then one line per host with its open ports.

docs.title: Interfaces, cables, vendor, icons
docs.text:
• Interfaces have a name (eth0, vmbr0, ge-0/0/1; was "label"), a type (ethernet, wifi, bond, bridge, vlan, virtual, wireguard, loopback, other) and more addresses (secondary IPs, as chips). Secondary addresses go into the host's firewall aliases, count as used in IPAM and in Discovery, and get no DNS records.
  • Logical stack: an interface can sit on another one: a VLAN on a bond, bond members on the bond, a bridge on a NIC, a VM's NIC on its hypervisor's bridge (srv-pm-pve-01:vmbr0). Lint warns when a VM NIC sits on a bridge that doesn't exist.
  • Cables: port here ⟷ other host's port, with medium (copper, fiber, DAC, Wi-Fi, virtual), speed and notes. A cable is stored once and shows on both hosts; the other end needn't be a known interface (switch ports usually aren't). Plugging a port that already has a cable moves it. The Network tab draws the stack with its cables.
  • Hosts have a vendor, a model and an icon (twenty kinds of device; by default from the type part of the name: vm, pm, fw, sw, ap, nas, …). Hosts are listed with their icon. Assigning a discovered address to a host fills its vendor (from the MAC) when empty, and "New host" from Discovery prefills it.
  • The Network tab shows, per address, what Discovery saw: name, vendor, MAC, source and when, with one-click "use as vendor" and "use" for the MAC. API: host seen.
  • YAML: interface kind, parent, extra_ips; host vendor, model, icon and cables (each cable once).

docs.title: Tags, naming lists, hosts
docs.text:
• Tags are known everywhere: hosts pick them from a list as chips (type to filter, Enter or comma to add, Backspace to remove); typing a new one adds it to the list. Naming → Tags lists them with colour, description and how many hosts carry them; renaming follows every host and tag: role scope, deleting removes the tag from its hosts. Existing host tags become the list on upgrade. YAML: tags: (those with a colour or description). API: /api/tags.
  • Naming has tabs (hostname parts, fun name pools, tags) and a search. Long lists show the first 12 with "Show all"; pools page through 15 at a time and show the names as chips, used ones struck through, matches highlighted while you search.
  • Hosts: Devices and VIPs in their own tabs (with counts; "+ VIP" opens the form as a VIP), and a tag filter.
  • The sidebar's zone tree scrolls under its pinned "Zones" header and search box.
  • Widget errors wrap and stay short (full text on hover).

docs.title: Zones made one by one
docs.text:
• An area is where something is; zones are made one by one inside it, each with a name, a rank (higher = more trusted; empty = none), a colour and a description. No more grid of every area × trust level.
  • Every area has a default zone with the area's own code (DC) for networks, hosts and interfaces you don't classify further. It has no rank, so the placement check leaves it alone. On the firewall it is NG_ZONE_DC_DEFAULT (NG_ZONE_DC stays the whole area).
  • Colours: pick one per area and, optionally, per zone (otherwise the area's). Chips, the sidebar and the matrix use them; the prompt and banner get the nearest terminal colour.
  • Renaming an area or zone renames it on networks, hosts, alias members, zone policy cells and role scopes. A zone in use, or named in the policy, can't be deleted.
  • Upgrading: every area gets its default zone, and each area × trust level combination in use becomes a zone named ", " with that level's rank, colour and description. Unused combinations are dropped, and so are trust levels.
  • YAML: zones: (code, name, rank, colour, description) and colour on areas. Files with trust_levels: still import, the same way as the upgrade.
  • The host page picks the home zone from one list grouped by area.
  • API: /api/zones/zones[/<code>] replaces /api/zones/trust; /api/meta zones carry area, rank, default and hex.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Feature variables: lists now merge (the parent's items first, then the ones a child adds) instead of the child's list replacing the parent's. {$replace: [...]} still replaces a list or mapping outright.
  • MAC addresses in Discovery come only from ARP/NDP tables and DHCP leases (OPNsense, Kea, UniFi). nmap no longer records them: behind a container bridge or a router it sees the wrong MAC. MACs that scans learned before are forgotten on upgrade.
  • Technitium: Conditional Forwarder zones are found and written like primary zones, so records go into e.g. mgmt.local.example.net when that is a forwarder zone.
  • Next free address skips addresses Discovery has seen (scans, ARP/NDP, leases, DNS), IPv6 interface ids included.
  • Custom records may be wildcards: *.primary.docker (only as the leftmost label).
  • Tabs no longer show a vertical scrollbar.

docs.title: Demo mode
docs.text:
• LABDEX_DEMO=1: loads a sample lab (networks, hosts, services, aliases, a zone policy) into an empty database and again every night at 03:00 UTC, with a demo admin whose password is on the sign-in page and a banner saying when it resets.
  • The built-in Demo lab plugin, only there in demo mode, is a pretend DNS server (plan, approve, apply) and monitor (one host has a bad day), with dashboard and host widgets. Nothing in the demo reaches a network: other plugins can't be added or run, ctx.http and Ansible refuse, and plugin installs, repositories, notification channels, secrets, restores, user and password changes are off.

docs.title: Plugin compatibility
docs.text:
• labdex: in plugin.yaml names the labdex versions a plugin works with, as a PEP 440 range (">=1.0", ">=1.0,<2"). labdex refuses to install a plugin outside its range, doesn't load an installed one that falls outside after an upgrade, and says why. No range: assumed to work.
  • Repository indexes carry the range; the marketplace shows it and doesn't offer plugins that need another labdex. The plugin page shows "works with".
  • From 1.0 on the plugin API only grows within a major version (see the README).

docs.title: Public services
docs.text:
• A service can be public: tick it, give it a public name (dns.example.com) and a WAN port. Public services need a port; lint warns when one lives outside a DMZ zone and notes a public service without a name.
  • OPNsense "Sync port forwards" plans one destination NAT rule per public service (WAN address and port → the host's address and the service's port), in the category automation:labdex, keyed [nat:host/service]. Rules you made yourself are never touched. The WAN interface and destination are settings.
  • Technitium split horizon (setting, on by default): each public name becomes a zone on the internal server with the service's internal addresses, so inside the house the name resolves to the host and not to the WAN address. The zone is created as part of the plan. Public DNS stays with whoever hosts it; labdex doesn't touch it.
  • The policy page of an OPNsense instance has a Zones table: per zone, the labdex rules, other pass rules on its interfaces and access-check gaps. A zone with only labdex rules and no gaps is "managed by labdex". "Check access" logs those zones.

docs.title: Firewall rules from the zone matrix
docs.text:
• OPNsense "Sync policy rules" (plan/apply) turns every matrix cell into pass rules on the source zone's interfaces, between the zones' aliases, with port aliases or tcp/443-style ports. A service's allow from that the matrix doesn't already cover gets a rule of its own. All of them live in the category automation:labdex, keyed in the description; nothing else on the firewall is changed.
  • "Rules no policy explains" lists your own pass rules between zones that the matrix doesn't allow. It's on the instance's Firewall policy page.
  • The rules are re-planned after inventory and policy changes, and wait for approval.

docs.title: Zone policy
docs.text:
• New Policy page: a matrix of zones, rows where traffic comes from, columns where it goes. A cell holds ports (any, port aliases, tcp/22, udp/53, ranges) and a reason. Anything not listed is denied.
  • Everyone can read it; admins edit it. Changes are recorded in History (type zone_policy), emit policy.updated and are part of the YAML export and import (zone_policy).

docs.title: Routing discovery
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin for OPNsense with FRR (its diagnostics API) or Cisco IOS-XE (RESTCONF: the BGP operational model and the ietf-routing table). "Read routes and neighbours" lists BGP neighbours (matched to hosts), the routed prefixes that aren't an inventory network, and the inventory networks the router has no route for. Default and host routes are left out; prefixes that are fine without a network can be ignored.
  • A neighbour that drops out of Established sends plugin.routing.neighbour_down. A Routing page and a dashboard widget show it.

docs.title: UniFi Network
docs.text: • New built-in plugin using UniFi's integration API (an API key, UniFi Network 9 or newer). Clients go into Discovery with address, MAC and name; UniFi devices (switches, access points, gateways) that are in the inventory report online or offline as host status. A dashboard widget lists the devices.

docs.title: Tailscale and Headscale
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read devices" puts every tailnet device's addresses into Discovery, so unknown ones can be assigned to hosts (e.g. in a 100.64.0.0/10 network in your remote-access area). Devices that are hosts report online as status; offline counts as no data unless you choose "down".
  • Widgets: the tailnet on the dashboard; a host's device, addresses, OS and key expiry on its page.

docs.title: k3s / Kubernetes
docs.text: • New built-in plugin, read-only with a service account token. "Read nodes" matches nodes to hosts, reports Ready / NotReady as host status, and lists drift against the cluster's feature (hosts with the feature that aren't nodes, nodes without it), nodes that match no host, and mixed kubelet versions. A Cluster page, a dashboard widget and a node widget on the host page.

docs.title: Proxmox VE (read-only)
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin with a read-only API token (PVEAuditor). "Import guests" plans one host per VM or container labdex doesn't know: a guest named by the convention keeps its name; any other gets srv-vm-<name>-NN (ct for containers) with its Proxmox name as a fun name. It brings the node as "runs on", the MACs, the VLAN's network and the addresses from the guest agent (VMs) or the container. Guests that match an existing host by MAC, address or name are linked to it instead. Templates are skipped unless you want them. Applying records each import in History.
  • "Check drift" (hourly by default) compares every linked guest with its host: name, MACs, addresses, node, and running vs. the host's status, and lists guests not in the inventory. A host setting "Known differences" explains drift, which then doesn't count. A Proxmox page, a dashboard widget and a host widget show it.
  • labdex never changes anything in Proxmox; creating guests comes after 1.0.

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
• New built-in module. "Check certificates" (twice a day by default) connects to every https service in the inventory (by its link, or its address) and to other endpoints you list (mail.example.net:993), reads the certificate even when it isn't trusted, and records who it's for, the issuer, the expiry and whether it verifies.
  • Warns at 21 days and calls it critical at 7 (both adjustable): a plugin.certificates.expiring notification once per certificate and level, a Certificates page, a dashboard widget (soonest first) and a host widget.
  • The dashboard's Hosts tile counts active hosts no monitoring plugin reports on.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin over Uptime Kuma's own (socket.io) API. "Sync monitors" plans one monitor per service with a link (or, optionally, a port check for every TCP service) on the hosts the instance applies to, and changes or removes the ones labdex made when services change (they're marked labdex:<host>/<service> in their description; your own monitors are left alone). It runs after host changes, as a plan that goes through approvals. New monitors get the notification ids you list and certificate-expiry notifications.
  • "Read status" reports each host (up if a monitor of it is up, down if all are down) and each service: the Services page and its status dots now prefer a monitor over Discovery and say where the status came from. Monitors labdex didn't make count for the host their URL or address points at.
  • Widgets: all monitors on the dashboard (down first), a host's monitors on its page.
  • Needs python-socketio (the uptimekuma extra; in the Docker image).

docs.title: Beszel
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read host status" reports each host whose Beszel system (matched by address or name) is up or down, with CPU, memory and disk.
  • "Add hosts as systems" plans a Beszel system for every host the instance applies to that the hub doesn't know yet (address from a host setting or the primary interface). "Install the agent" (a host action) runs Beszel's install script over Ansible with the hub key, or a universal token for agents that connect themselves.
  • Widgets: every system on the dashboard (down first); CPU, memory, disk, load, uptime and agent version on each host.

docs.title: Host status from monitoring
docs.text:
• Status plugins report what they know about hosts. A host's status: down if any source says down, up if at least one says up, otherwise what Discovery last saw. A report older than "Monitoring reports are fresh for … minutes" (General, 15 by default) counts as no data.
  • The host list has a status dot and a column per source; the sidebar tree and the dashboard use the same status; a host's Plugins tab lists each source with its detail and since when.
  • When an active host goes from up to down or back, a host.down / host.up notification goes out (Discovery alone never sends one).
  • For plugin authors: ctx.report_status({host: {"state", "detail", "data"}}) and ctx.match_host(), which maps an address, name, FQDN (any generated DNS name), URL or host:port to an inventory host.

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus
docs.text:
• New built-in plugin. "Read host status" (every 2 minutes by default) asks the status query (up), matches each target's instance label to a host and reports it down when every target of the host is down. Basic or bearer authentication.
  • Widgets: "Targets down" on the dashboard; CPU over the last 6 hours (and memory) on each host, from node_exporter queries you can change.
  • Schedulable actions may set a default interval in the manifest (schedule_default).

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
• Plugins can show widgets on the dashboard and on a host's overview. They return data in fixed kinds (stat, status, list, table, sparkline) and labdex draws them: no plugin code runs in the browser, unknown kinds and fields are dropped and links must stay inside labdex or go to http(s). Results are cached per widget (refresh) and a slow or broken widget shows an error without holding up the page.
  • Host widgets appear only where the instance applies to the host, and only to people who can see both.
  • Built in: Backup → "Last backup" on the dashboard (age, kept, encrypted or not); nmap → "Open ports" on each host (documented or not).
  • API: GET /api/widgets, GET /api/hosts/<name>/widgets. Manifest: widgets: with id, label, where (dashboard, host), size (small, wide), refresh.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
• One Plugins section replaces Integrations. The sidebar's "Plugins" page shows every plugin with what it brings (actions, plans, exports, hooks, pages, host, endpoints, widgets, Ansible: read from its manifest) and its instances, filtered to the ones in use. Each plugin has its own page with its instances, actions, hooks and recent jobs; an instance (what used to be called an integration) keeps its page and settings. /integrations redirects; the API keeps its names.
  • GET /api/plugins/<id>; /api/plugins lists each plugin's instances and capabilities.

docs.title: Signed repositories
docs.text:
• Marketplace URLs are replaced by repositories: a signed index.json on any web server. The repository's key signs the index and every plugin in it. Adding one shows its name and key id first; the key is pinned, so a changed or re-signed index and plugins signed with another key are refused. Removing a repository stops the plugins only it vouched for. Indexes signed with the labdex project key show as official.
  • labdex plugin repo SOURCE OUTPUT --key KEY --name NAME signs every plugin folder, zips them and writes the signed index, ready to publish.
  • Unsigned marketplace URLs from 0.6 are no longer used; Admin → Plugins lists them.
  • API: /api/plugin-repos (/preview, then POST with the key id); /api/marketplace lists the repositories' plugins; install with {repository_id, id}.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
• A start page (/, "Dashboard" in the sidebar): hosts (up, down, planned), networks, services, lint and Discovery at a glance; plans waiting for approval (yours first) and approved plans waiting for their window; what's failing (the newest run of each action in the last week, until it succeeds again) and what's running; the last changes; scheduled templates and change windows coming up; hosts per zone; a warning when no worker runs jobs or notifications can't be delivered.
  • Everything on it follows your permissions. GET /api/dashboard.
  • Plugin widgets on the dashboard come with the plugin rework in 0.7.

docs.title: Ansible Vault and secrets in variables
docs.text:
• Feature and host variables can point at a global secret instead of holding it: admin_password: {$secret: grafana-admin}. The value is filled in only when labdex runs Ansible (in a private temporary folder) and never reaches the inventory, the YAML export, the API or History. Secret values are masked as ******** in job logs, --diff output included.
  • Ansible runner: "Ansible Vault password" (and an optional vault id) for files in your playbooks that are encrypted with ansible-vault.
  • File exports: with a vault password, the Ansible inventory export writes secrets as !vault values (Ansible's own format, 1.1 or 1.2 with a vault id), so a playbook run outside labdex decrypts them with the same password. Without one they stay references.
  • Lint: secret-missing when variables point at a secret that doesn't exist. The Secrets page lists features and hosts among "used by".
  • Secret settings of an integration no longer appear in labdex_settings.

docs.title: Job templates
docs.text:
• An action with its parameters (and host, for host actions) saved under a name, on the integration's page: run it with one click, or on a schedule (every N minutes, or on chosen days at a time in a time zone). Scheduled plans go through approvals like any other plan.
  • Running a template needs the right to apply the integration (and the host); a schedule, which runs unattended, needs admin rights on the integration. Jobs show the template they came from. API: /api/job-templates (+ /run).

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
• Channels (Admin → Notifications): ntfy (server, topic, optional token, priority), Matrix (homeserver, room id or alias, access token), email (SMTP with STARTTLS/SSL) and webhooks (JSON body; with a secret, an X-Labdex-Signature: sha256=… HMAC). Each picks its events and, optionally, which integrations it hears about.
  • Events: plan.waiting (needs approval), plan.applied, job.failed, backup.failed, host.down / host.up (for status integrations), test. Plugins send their own with ctx.notify(…), as plugin.<id>.<event>.
  • An outbox: messages go out from the worker, and failed ones are retried after 1, 5, 15 and 60 minutes. "Recently sent" lists them with the error; each channel shows its last message and how many failed. A Test button sends one right away and says what went wrong.
  • New setting "Address of this labdex" (General) for links back to the job.

docs.title: Approvals and change windows
docs.text:
• Approval policies (Admin → Approvals & windows). A plan is matched, top to bottom, by integration name, the zones of the hosts it runs for and how it was started (by someone, by a hook, on a schedule). The policy sets the approvals needed (0 = applies by itself), who may give them (users and @groups; empty = anyone who may apply the integration), whether whoever started the plan may approve it, a delay after planning, and a change window. Without a match it's as before: you approve your own plans.
  • Change windows: weekly times in a time zone (e.g. Tue and Thu 20:00–22:00 Europe/Berlin; a window may run past midnight). An approved plan waits as "approved" until its delay has passed and its window is open; the worker applies it.
  • A plan the inventory has moved past is planned again when it's approved or its window opens. If the new plan has the same changes, the approvals carry over; if not, it waits for approval again. A newer plan for the same action keeps the approvals of the one it replaces the same way.
  • The job page shows the policy, the approvals with comments, why you can't approve (not an approver, you started it, already approved), and when an approved plan applies. Approved plans can still be discarded, with a comment.
  • API: POST /api/jobs/<id>/approve {comment} (/apply does the same, for older clients), /discard {comment}; /api/approval-policies (with PUT …/order) and /api/change-windows. Approvals are recorded in History.
  • labdex action … --apply on the command line still applies right away.

docs.title: Worker and run history
docs.text:
• Jobs are a queue in the database. A dispatcher claims a job, runs it and sends heartbeats; a job whose worker stops (no heartbeat for 90 seconds) is marked failed instead of hanging in "running".
  • New labdex worker [--slots N]: runs queued jobs and the scheduler in its own process. With LABDEX_WORKER=external the web server only queues jobs (Ansible runs and scans stay out of the web process, and several gunicorn workers on PostgreSQL become possible). The default, inline, keeps everything in one container. docker-compose.yml has a commented worker service.
  • About shows who runs jobs, the workers seen in the last minute and how many jobs wait; a queued job says when no worker is there to pick it up. GET /api/jobs/queue.
  • Run history per host: a "Runs" tab lists the jobs that ran for the host (host actions and Ansible runs that included it), and follows renames. GET /api/jobs?host=NAME; jobs list their hosts and worker.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A service has a description, "listens on" (every address, the primary interface, one network, or one address) and, for web links, "link by name or address".
  • Discovery ("missing services") and the OPNsense firewall access check only look at the addresses a service listens on.
  • "Allow from" is picked from zones, areas, networks and aliases (/api/services/sources); sources labdex doesn't know are marked, and lint warns about them (allow-from-unknown).
  • The Services page is a launcher: cards grouped by zone with an Open button, status from Discovery (answering / not answering / not scanned), filters and a table view.

docs.title: IPv6 discovery
docs.text:
• OPNsense "Import ARP and NDP tables": IPv6 neighbours (diagnostics/interface/getNdp) with their MACs, next to ARP.
  • OPNsense "Import DHCP leases": Kea DHCPv6 address leases too (kea/leases6/search); delegated-prefix leases (IA_PD) are left out.
  • nmap: "Also scan known IPv6 addresses" (on by default). A /64 can't be swept, so it scans the IPv6 addresses of the inventory's hosts and those Discovery learned inside the chosen networks' IPv6 prefixes, with nmap -6, after the IPv4 sweep.
  • Link-local, multicast and loopback addresses never enter Discovery.

docs.title: Prefix delegation
docs.text:
• OPNsense: new action "Read delegated IPv6 prefixes" (schedulable). It reads the prefix each WAN interface received (interfaces/overview/interfaces_info, ifctl.prefix) and moves every delegated network prefix to its subnet: prefix ID N of size /L inside the delegation.
  • A change is recorded in the network's history ("delegated prefix A → B") and announced, so host GUA addresses (interface ID × prefix), AAAA records and N6/H6 aliases follow on the next sync.
  • Delegated prefixes that don't fit (prefix ID too large) or whose WAN interface reports nothing are listed in the job log and left alone.

docs.title: IPv6 host addresses
docs.text:
• Each interface has an IPv6 interface ID (::53, or eui64 from the MAC). It is used in every IPv6 prefix of the network, so adding a GUA prefix gives every host its GUA address at once. An explicit address stays valid and stands for the prefix it lies in; a per-prefix override wins over both.
  • One AAAA record per prefix; H6 aliases, Discovery, lint (duplicates), Ansible (ip6_all), Prometheus targets and the firewall access check use every address.
  • The host form shows the addresses an interface gets while you type, offers the next free interface ID, and has per-prefix overrides under "per prefix…".
  • Network usage lists the next free interface IDs of each IPv6 prefix.

docs.title: Networks: address families
docs.text:
• A network has any number of prefixes, IPv4 and IPv6 (e.g. a ULA and a GUA). Each has a mask from a list, an optional gateway and DHCP range, given as a full address or a suffix (254 → .254, ::1), and a description.
  • IPv6 prefixes can be marked "delegated": from a WAN interface with a prefix ID and length. Resolving the live prefix from OPNsense comes in 0.5.7.
  • Overlaps inside a network and with other networks are refused.
  • Firewall network aliases (N4/N6) hold every prefix of their family; host addresses may sit in any prefix; Discovery, nmap targets and the firewall access check use all of them.
  • The Usage tab shows every prefix: addresses in use, DHCP pool, next free (IPv4).
  • The old single-prefix fields stay in the API and mirror the first prefix of each family. YAML stays short for simple networks and lists prefixes otherwise.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Firewall access check: only inbound rules can grant access. OPNsense lists its built-in "let out anything from firewall host itself" with direction out and no source or destination, which labdex read as any → any. Outbound rules still show in the host's rule list, marked "out".

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: • The network page has tabs: Overview (settings, aliases), Usage (addresses in use, next free) and Hosts (every host with an interface there, its addresses and MACs, and whether its home zone differs).

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: • The rest of v0.5 is split into small releases: address families (0.5.5), IPv6 host addresses (0.5.6), prefix delegation (0.5.7), IPv6 discovery (0.5.8), services (0.5.9). Dashboard, plugins rework, widgets and routing discovery are placed in v0.6 to v0.8.

docs.title: DNS zones
docs.text:
• A network can have a DNS zone of its own: empty = <host>.<network>.<domain> as before, @ = <host>.<domain>, or e.g. home.lab = <host>.home.lab.
  • A host can have a main DNS zone for its short name, fun names, service names and extra records (default: the domain). Address records follow their network.
  • Two networks in the same zone give a host distinct names (<host>-<network>); with @, the short name is the address record itself (no CNAME beside it).
  • The BIND export writes one $ORIGIN block per zone; conflicts are checked by full name.

docs.title: Service records
docs.text: • DNS-SD (_service._proto SRV + TXT) is now a checkbox per service, off for new services. Services from before 0.5.3 keep theirs.

docs.title: Technitium
docs.text:
• Syncs every zone labdex writes into. Each record goes into the closest zone that exists on the server; names without a zone there are listed in the job log.
  • "Extra zones to read" for import and the host panel (never written). The old single "Zone" setting still works and is read like an extra zone.
  • Works without permission to list zones (falls back to labdex's own zones).

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
• MACs: nmap records them when it runs as root on the segment; after every scan the scanning machine's ARP table fills in the rest; ARP and Kea leases keep doing it too. Each MAC remembers where it came from.
  • New "MACs" tab: interfaces in the inventory without a MAC whose address was seen with one, filled in with one click (one history entry per host). VIPs are left out.
  • Open ports show the address's MAC and vendor.

docs.title: Sidebar
docs.text: • Only the zone tree scrolls, with its scrollbar space reserved: opening and closing zones no longer changes the sidebar's width.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Zones and Naming have their own sidebar entries (out of Admin); everyone can look, administrators change them. Features is always in the sidebar.
  • The role part of a hostname (srv-vm-<role>-01) is free text. The builder suggests defined roles and those already in use; defining one only adds a label.
  • The host field "role" is now function ("DNS resolver"), to stop the clash with the hostname's role. Older YAML files and API clients that send role still work; Ansible gets labdex_function (labdex_role stays until 0.7).
  • Fun name pools: four neutral built-ins (Greek gods, stars, trees, minerals) plus your own (paste a list). A pool can apply to categories, areas or zones; "Suggest" on the host form offers unused names from the matching pool.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
• Each host has a DNS tab: extra records (alias CNAME, A/AAAA, TXT, SRV, MX) with placeholders ({target}, {fqdn}, {ip4}, {ip6}, {host}, {fun}), and a switch per fun name to publish it or not.
  • An alias with an empty value points at the primary record, so it follows when the primary interface changes.
  • These records are part of the inventory (YAML, exports, Technitium sync). The Technitium module's per-host "extra records" moved here on upgrade.

docs.title: About
docs.text: • About page (user menu, Admin → General): version, schema, database, plugins with versions and trust, and this changelog. Optional check for new releases on GitHub (off by default; Admin → General).

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
• A host's home zone now follows its primary interface's network (or the first interface in a network). Choose "pin" to keep a zone of your own. When a network changes zone, hosts that follow it move along, with a history entry.
  • Zone is picked as area + trust level. New hosts no longer default to a zone that may not exist.
  • Every address shows its network's zone. Someone who may see a zone can now view (not edit) hosts with an address there, e.g. the edge firewall for a DMZ-only user. The sidebar puts such hosts in the zone they can see.
  • Upgrading pins exactly the hosts whose zone differed from their network.

docs.title: VIPs
docs.text:
• New host kind "VIP": a shared address with a protocol (CARP, VRRP, keepalived, kube-vip, MetalLB, anycast) and member hosts. It gets DNS, firewall aliases and services like any host. Members list it on their Network tab and get labdex_vips plus a vip_<name> group in Ansible. The VIP itself is never an Ansible target and has no MAC. Hostname type vip added.
  • Member renames and deletions are followed; YAML import/export keeps members.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text:
• Host pickers (Discovery "add to host…", VIP members) are no longer cut off by the table; full names, keyboard selection, flips upwards near the bottom.
  • Migrations on SQLite run with foreign keys off, so rebuilding a table can't cascade-delete interfaces.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
• OPNsense and Technitium calls checked against the sources of OPNsense 26.1 (Kea inside OPNsense) and Technitium DNS Server 15.6.2; contract tests pin them.
  • OPNsense grid searches POST rowCount: -1 (all rows) and fall back to GET.
  • Firewall rules are recognised as labdex's by the UUID of the automation:labdex category, which is what OPNsense returns.
  • Technitium: the API token goes in Authorization: Bearer, not the form body; the host panel matches every fun name of a host.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
• UI query cache (stale-while-revalidate): pages show the last answer at once and refresh in the background; every change, from any tab or the CLI, arrives on the event stream (revision) and refreshes what's on screen.
  • List pages stay alive: back from a host keeps filters, search and rows.
  • Host links prefetch on hover; saving a host writes the answer into the cache.
  • The host picker loads four fields instead of whole hosts.
  • Host list renders 200 rows at a time; search no longer matches field names.
  • Server: weak ETags with 304 Not Modified on every GET; a per-revision host index behind the host list, sidebar and counts (1000 hosts: host list 45 ms, sidebar 60 ms, slim list 5 ms).
  • /api/hosts: fields, q, zone, status, sort, limit/offset (X-Total-Count); cursor paging on history and jobs (X-Next-Before).
  • Static files: hashed assets cached for a year, precompressed .br/.gz.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
