• Alembic migrations, run on start; a 0.4 database is adopted automatically.
  • PostgreSQL support (optional; SQLite stays the default). The test suite runs on both.
  • labdex db current | upgrade | copy --to URL (move SQLite → PostgreSQL).
  • Backups carry a portable database.json and restore into either database.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
• GitHub Actions: tests on SQLite and PostgreSQL, browser tests (Playwright), a performance budget on 1000 generated hosts, Docker build; multi-arch images to GHCR on tags.
  • tools/big_inventory.py makes large test inventories.
  • Fixed: a hook-triggered re-run raised an error after starting the job.

Editable zones, discovery workflow (adopt, assign, paging, Kea leases and DNS records as sources), Server-Sent Events, sidebar with zone tree and module menu, plugin store with signatures and trust levels, host page tabs, dotted service DNS names, per-interface DNS, admin panel, Kea reservations, firewall aliases by id in automation:labdex, hostname builder, multiple fun names.
Module framework with selectors and per-host settings, Technitium DNS, OPNsense aliases and access checks, Ansible runner with features, secrets vault, backups (folder and S3).
Users, groups, roles and scopes, change history with revert, plugins with plan/apply, nmap discovery.

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
JSON under /api; sign in with the session cookie (browser; writes also need the header X-Requested-With: labdex) or a bearer token. Validation errors come back as 422 with a list of {field, message}; missing permissions as 403; objects outside your scope as 404.

Every successful GET carries a weak ETag; send it back as If-None-Match and an unchanged answer is an empty 304. Lists page with a cursor: /api/history and /api/jobs take limit and before=<id> and return the next cursor in X-Next-Before. /api/hosts takes fields=name,zone,…, q=, zone=, status=, sort=name|-zone|ip|…, limit= and offset=, with the total in X-Total-Count.

Hosts, networks and zones carry a uid (ten characters, never changes); every path that takes a host or network name (/api/hosts/<name>, /api/networks/<name>, …) takes the uid as well, so scripts that keep ids survive renames.

Method Path GET /api/meta Zones, areas, settings, counts, your permissions GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/hosts · /api/hosts/<name> Hosts (filtered to what you may see; can_edit per row) GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/networks · /api/networks/<name> Networks; /next gives the next free address GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/dashboards · /api/dashboards/<uid> Dashboards: {name, shared, items: [{type, x, y, w, h, config}]}; shared ones need an administrator GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/racks · /api/racks/<name or uid> Racks with the hosts in them; PUT/DELETE /api/racks/<rack>/hosts/<host> {unit, height, face} places or takes out a host; POST /api/racks/<rack>/items, PUT/DELETE …/items/<id> {kind, label, description, unit, height, face} for panels GET · POST /api/vault · /api/vault/{init,unseal,seal,passphrase} The vault's state (initialized, sealed, reauth_needed); setting it up, unsealing, sealing, a new passphrase (administrators) GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/vault/entries?host=&q= · /api/vault/entries/<uid> Secrets by name: {path, host, description, fields: {name: value}}; values are never in these answers. In PUT, a field's value null keeps it, fields left out go POST /api/vault/entries/<uid>/reveal · /api/auth/confirm {field, version?} → {value}, needs secret:apply, written to History; a browser session confirms its password first ({password}, every 5 minutes, else 403 with field password) GET · POST · POST /api/cables/suggestions · /api/cables/suggestions/accept · /api/cables/suggestions/ignore Cables switches see: suggested, conflicts (with what's now on record), unknown neighbours; accept {keys, replace}, ignore {keys} GET /api/cables Every cable you may see both ends of, with label, length (metres), colour; and next_label GET, POST · PUT, DELETE /api/topology/views · /api/topology/views/<uid> Saved topology views: {name, config: {view, zone, hidden_nets, lonely, grid, camera: {zoom, x, y}}} GET /api/zones/zones/<code or uid> One zone: its networks, hosts at home there, policy cells from and to it GET, PUT · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/topology?view=physical\|l3 · /api/topology/layout, /api/topology/cables[/<id>] The pictures, their shared arrangement, cables drawn on the map (both ends may be one host, on different ports); PUT …/cables/<id> {medium, speed, notes} changes one GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/aliases[/<name>] Aliases, generated and custom GET /api/services, /api/lint Services, convention checks GET · GET · POST /api/history · /api/history/<id> · /api/history/<id>/revert Audit log with diffs GET /api/discovery/{summary,services,missing,unknown-hosts} Discovery GET, POST · GET, PUT, DELETE /api/integrations · /api/integrations/<name> Integration instances POST /api/integrations/<name>/actions/<action> Start a job (202) GET /api/integrations/<name>/export/<action>, /endpoints/<id> Exports, plugin endpoints GET · POST /api/jobs[/<id>] · /api/jobs/<id>/{apply,discard} Jobs and plans GET · PUT /api/hosts/<name>/modules · /api/hosts/<name>/modules/<integration> Integrations for a host: on/off, host settings GET · POST …/modules/<integration>/view · …/actions/<action> Host panel, host actions GET, POST · PUT, DELETE /api/features · /api/features/<path> Feature tree GET · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/zones · /api/zones/{areas,trust}[/<code>] Areas and trust levels; POST /api/zones/example GET · GET · POST, PUT, DELETE /api/naming · /api/naming/next?category=&type=&role= · /api/naming/<kind>[/<code>] Hostname parts, next free name GET, POST · PUT, DELETE · GET /api/naming/pools · /api/naming/pools/<name> · /api/naming/fun-suggest?category=&zone=&pool= Fun name pools, unused suggestions GET /api/about Version, schema, database, plugins, changelog GET /api/nav Sidebar: zone tree with live status, which pages to show GET /api/events[?job=<id>] Server-Sent Events: plan count, revision on every change, job status and output POST · POST · DELETE /api/plugins/upload · /api/plugins/stage/<token>/confirm · /api/plugins/<id> Install, confirm, remove GET · POST /api/plugin-repos (/preview) Signed repositories GET /api/marketplace (?offline=1 skips the repositories) Everything installable: what repositories offer (installed, update, repo_version), and development checkouts (bundled) POST /api/marketplace/install {repository_id, id} Stages a repository plugin for /api/plugins/stage/<token>/confirm (a development checkout, {id}, installs at once) DELETE /api/plugins/<id> Uninstall (409 while it has instances) POST /api/plugins/restore Install the plugins this labdex uses but doesn't have (after an upgrade from 1.24.0) from the official repository now: {installed, failed, missing}; GET /api/plugins lists them as missing POST · DELETE /api/discovery/addresses/assign · /api/discovery/addresses/<ip> Add a seen address to a host; forget it GET · PUT, DELETE /api/secrets · /api/secrets/<name> The older API for vault entries under global/ (field value); writing needs the vault unsealed GET /api/vault/refs The fields you may point plugins and Ansible variables at: vault:<path>#<field> GET /api/dashboard, /api/widgets, /api/hosts/<name>/widgets Start page, widgets GET · PUT /api/zone-policy Zone matrix (PUT one cell: {src, dst, ports, description}; admins) POST /api/jobs/<id>/approve, /api/jobs/<id>/discard {comment} GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/approval-policies, /api/change-windows Approvals and windows (PUT /api/approval-policies/order) GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/notification-channels (/<id>/test), /api/notifications Notifications GET, POST, PUT, DELETE /api/job-templates (/<id>/run) Job templates GET /api/plugins/<id>, /api/jobs/queue Plugin details, the job queue /api/auth/*, /api/admin/* Sign-in, tokens; users, groups, roles, bindings, grants, backup/restore

Within 1.x, fields and endpoints are added, not removed or renamed (Upgrading).

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
labdex import inventory.yaml       # replace the inventory (asks first; --yes to skip)
labdex export -o inventory.yaml    # write the inventory
labdex lint                        # exit 1 on errors; --warnings-as-errors for strict CI
labdex user create NAME [--admin]  # labdex user password NAME
labdex token create USER NAME [--read-only] [--days 90]
labdex plugins                     # plugins and integrations
labdex action fw-main sync_aliases [--apply]
labdex worker [--slots N]          # run jobs (LABDEX_WORKER=external)
labdex backup create -o FILE | check FILE | restore FILE [--inventory-only]
labdex db current | upgrade | copy --to URL
labdex plugin keygen | sign | pack | repo

Every command reads the same environment as the server (LABDEX_DATA, LABDEX_DB).

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Issues, pull requests and the licence of contributions: see CONTRIBUTING.md. Security problems: SECURITY.md, never in a public issue. How branches, versions and releases work: Branches, versions and releases.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
cd backend && pip install -e ".[server,postgres,uptimekuma,test]" ruff
pytest -q                                                       # SQLite
LABDEX_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://u@localhost/t pytest -q   # the same suite on PostgreSQL
LABDEX_E2E=1 pytest -q tests/e2e                                # browser tests (build the UI, playwright install chromium)
LABDEX_PERF=1 pytest -q -s tests/test_perf.py                   # performance budget, 1000 hosts
ruff check labdex tools tests                                   # pyflakes, pycodestyle, bugbear, pyupgrade
cd ../frontend && npm run lint                                  # ESLint: JavaScript and Vue rules (eslint.config.js)
cd ../frontend && npm ci && npm run dev                         # Vite on :5173, proxies /api to labdex run --debug
pip install mkdocs-material && mkdocs serve                     # these docs

Plugins for other systems are tested against small fake servers (tests/fakes.py) that follow the real API; tests/test_contracts.py pins the details that matter.

Official plugins live in their own repositories (labdex-plugin-<id>) and must have a labdex range, tests, and use nothing outside the plugin API. They aren't part of labdex and don't go into its image: plugins/ holds them as git submodules for development and the tests only (git clone --recurse-submodules). The tests load them through LABDEX_DEV_PLUGINS=plugins (set by tests/conftest.py); set it yourself to run a development server with them.

docs.title: Plugin API reference
docs.text: This is the stable plugin API of labdex 1.x: within a major version it only grows. Anything not listed here (other modules, models, private methods) may change.

docs.title: plugin.yaml

docs.title: Isolated plugins
docs.text:
Community and unsigned plugins run in a separate, locked-down process (see Installing plugins). For them:

  • self.ctx offers exactly the Context below; labdex's other modules aren't reachable (importing labdex.store works, but it has no database to talk to).
  • data_dir is the instance's own folder, kept between runs; the working directory and TMPDIR are a fresh temporary folder per call.
  • Everything you pass to labdex or return goes over JSON: keep return values to dicts, lists, strings, numbers, Change and ExportFile.
  • print() ends up in the job log.
  • Each call is a fresh process: keep state in set_state, not in module globals.
  • Calls time out after an hour (actions) or a minute (pages, widgets, endpoints).

Write plugins that only use this page, and they run the same either way.

docs.title: Writing a plugin
docs.text:
A plugin is a folder with plugin.yaml and, optionally, plugin.py and Ansible playbooks. Drop it into /data/plugins/<id>/ and restart (or Plugins → Reload).

# plugin.yaml
id: pihole
name: Pi-hole
kind: integration            # or module (exists once, no instances to add)
version: "0.1"
labdex: ">=1.0,<2"           # the labdex versions it works with (PEP 440 range)
description: Local DNS records in Pi-hole
applies_to: ["tag:pihole"]   # what a new instance applies to (default *); RBAC scope syntax
settings:
  - {key: url, label: URL, type: string, required: true}
  - {key: password, type: secret, required: true}
  - {key: networks, type: networks}          # string secret bool int select text list networks table yaml
  - {key: auth, type: select, default: token, options: [{value: token, label: API token}, {value: password, label: Password}]}
  - {key: token, type: secret, required: true, when: {auth: token}}   # only shown (and required) for that choice
host_settings:                               # per host, shown on the host page
  - {key: records, type: table, columns: [{key: name}, {key: value, required: true}]}
host_view: true                              # host_view(host) fills a panel on the host page
tags: [dns]
provides: [discovery]                        # shows the Discovery page (or: features)
pages:                                       # tabs on the integration, filled by page_<id>(args)
  - {id: overview, label: Pi-hole}
actions:
  - {id: test, label: Test connection, mode: run}
  - {id: sync, label: Sync records, mode: plan, schedulable: true}
  - {id: hosts_file, label: hosts file, mode: export}
  - {id: deploy, mode: plan, ansible: playbooks/deploy.yml}   # Ansible: check+diff, then apply
  - {id: restart, mode: run, scope: host, danger: true,       # per host, with a form for parameters
     params: [{key: service, type: string, required: true}]}
hooks:
  - {events: ["host.*", "network.*"], action: sync}
endpoints:
  - {id: targets, label: JSON for something to poll}
widgets:
  - {id: queries, label: DNS queries, where: dashboard, size: wide, refresh: 60}

# plugin.py
from labdex.plugins.base import Change, ExportFile, Plugin as Base, PluginError

class Plugin(Base):
    def run_test(self, params):
        self.ctx.http(self.settings["url"]).get("api/info")
        return {"message": "ok"}

    def plan_sync(self, params):           # a list of Change
        want = {r["fqdn"]: r for r in self.ctx.inventory.dns_records() if r["type"] == "A"}
        return [Change("create", "record", fqdn, f"A {r['value']}", after=r, data=r) for fqdn, r in want.items()]

    def apply_sync(self, changes, params):  # the reviewed plan
        for c in changes:
            self.log(f"creating {c.name}")
        return {"applied": len(changes)}

    def export_hosts_file(self, params):
        return ExportFile("hosts", "...", "text/plain")

    def endpoint_targets(self, params):
        return [...]

    def host_view(self, host):
        return {"summary": [{"label": "records", "value": 3, "tone": "ok"}],
                "sections": [{"title": "Records", "type": "table", "columns": [{"key": "name", "label": "Name"}],
                              "rows": [{"name": "nas", "_tone": "warn"}]}]}

    def widget_queries(self, host):         # host is None on the dashboard
        return {"kind": "sparkline", "points": [1, 3, 2], "unit": "q/s"}

Methods are found by name: run_<action>, plan_<action> and apply_<action>, export_<action>, endpoint_<id>, page_<id>, widget_<id>, host_view. Raise PluginError("…") for errors the user should read. The reference lists everything a plugin can use.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Run labdex locally (labdex run --debug) with LABDEX_PLUGIN_DIR pointing at your plugins folder. labdex's own tests use small fake servers for each API (backend/tests/fakes.py); the same pattern works for plugins.

docs.title: Sign and pack
docs.text:
labdex plugin keygen my.pem                      # my.pem (keep it secret) and my.pem.pub
labdex plugin sign ./pihole --key my.pem --signer "Your Name"
labdex plugin pack ./pihole -o pihole-0.1.zip

People trust your key under Plugins → Signing keys (paste my.pem.pub); then your plugin installs as community.

docs.title: A plugin in its own git repository
docs.text:
That's how labdex's own plugins live (labdex-plugin-<id>): the plugin at the root of a repository, released by publishing a GitHub release. Start one from a plugin folder:

python3 backend/tools/plugin_repo/make_plugin_repo.py ./pihole ../labdex-plugin-pihole --community

It adds a README from the manifest, a licence (MIT for your own plugins, change it as you like; AGPL-3.0 for official ones), a CHANGELOG and the release workflow. Set the repository secret LABDEX_SIGNING_KEY to your private key. Then each release is: bump version in plugin.yaml, add a ## <version> section to CHANGELOG.md, commit, then publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> (in the web UI, or gh release create v<version> --target main --notes ""). The workflow checks the tag against the manifest, signs exactly what's committed and attaches <id>-<version>.zip to the release with CHANGELOG.md; the release description gets that version's CHANGELOG section (below anything you wrote). Files listed in .releaseignore (one pattern per line, like .gitignore: tests/, *.log, docs/draft.md) stay out of the zip; so do the repository's own files (.git, .github, .gitignore). labdex plugin prune <copy> does that by hand.

docs.title: A Marketplace from plugin repositories
docs.text:
A Marketplace is a repository with a plugins.yaml:

name: My plugins
description: Plugins by me
plugins:
  - repo: me/labdex-plugin-pihole
    withdrawn: {"0.3": "loses the blocklists on restart"}

Add discover: [{owner: me, prefix: labdex-plugin-}] and every public repository of yours named like that is included too, so a new plugin repository shows up by itself.

labdex plugin build-index plugins.yaml site --key my.pem reads every listed repository's releases (with GITHUB_TOKEN set it can make more API calls), checks each archive's checksum and that it's signed with your key, and writes a signed site/index.json that points at the release assets. Every release is a version people can install, update to or go back to, with its notes; a withdrawn version stays installable on purpose but warns everyone who has it, and updates skip it. Publish site/ on GitHub Pages: the labdex-plugins repository is a ready-made example (it rebuilds every hour, when plugins.yaml changes, and on a plugin-released dispatch from a plugin's release workflow).

docs.title: A repository from plugin folders
docs.text:
Or put each plugin in its own folder and build a repository with the archives in it:

labdex plugin repo ./plugins ./public --key my.pem --name "My plugins" --description "…"

This signs every plugin, zips them and writes a signed public/index.json. Publish public/ on any web server (GitHub Pages works). People add the URL of index.json under Plugins → Repositories, compare the key id with the one you publish, and install from the marketplace. The key is pinned: changing it means people add the repository again.

Each index entry carries the plugin's labdex range, so the marketplace only offers plugins that work with the labdex looking at it. Building into a folder that already has an index keeps the older versions whose archives are still there, so people can go back to them; labdex plugin fetch-repo <url> <folder> --key my.pem downloads what's published first. A plugin folder's CHANGELOG.md (## <version> sections) gives each version its notes.

Withdraw a version (or undo it) and re-sign the index:

labdex plugin yank ./public pihole 0.3 --key my.pem --reason "loses the blocklists on restart"
labdex plugin yank ./public pihole 0.3 --key my.pem          # offered again

docs.title: The official Marketplace
docs.text: Every official plugin lives in its own repository (labdex-app/labdex-plugin-<id>); labdex has them as git submodules in plugins/ for its tests, but doesn't ship them: users install them from the Marketplace. labdex-plugins lists them; its index is signed with the project key and published at https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex-plugins/index.json, which labdex trusts out of the box. Contributions are welcome: see Contributing.

docs.title: labdex's own versions
docs.text:
labdex releases are MAJOR.MINOR.SUB; a hotfix of a release is MAJOR.MINOR.SUB-N:

Version What it is 1.9.0 a release 1.9.0-1, 1.9.0-2 its hotfixes: bug fixes only, they come after 1.9.0 1.9.1 a small release 1.10.0 the next release

A hotfix is what Python calls a post-release (1.9.0-1 is 1.9.0.post1), so plugin ranges like labdex: ">=1.9,<2" take hotfixes as you'd expect. The image of 1.9.0-1 is tagged 1.9.0-1, 1.9.0, 1.9, 1 and latest: a hotfix replaces its release.

To make one, python backend/tools/bump.py sub|minor|major|patch (or an exact version) writes the version everywhere and opens a changelog heading. Push that to main, then publish a GitHub release tagged v<version> on it (gh release create v1.23.0 --target main --notes ""): the release workflow builds and signs the image and the files and attaches them, with the changelog section as notes if you left them empty. It refuses a tag that doesn't match the code's version.

docs.title: Branches, versions and releases
docs.text:
labdex uses release branches: main is where the next version grows, a branch per minor version is where it's stabilised and later patched, and every release is a GitHub release on that branch.

main ──●──●──●──●──────●──●──●──●──────────●──●──▶  (next: 1.25)
          \                 \
           release/1.23      release/1.24 ──●──●──▶
            v1.23.0  v1.23.1   v1.24.0   v1.24.0-1

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
MAJOR.MINOR.SUB, plus -N for a hotfix:

Change Version Branch New features (a release) 1.24.0 release/1.24, cut from main Small additions, docs, CI, no migration 1.24.1 release/1.24 Bug fixes only 1.24.0-1, 1.24.0-2 release/1.24 Breaking changes (a database or API that older clients can't use) 2.0.0 release/2.0

A hotfix sorts after its release (Python calls 1.24.0-1 a post-release), so plugin ranges like labdex: ">=1.24,<2" include it. Its image takes the floating tags (1.24.0, 1.24, 1, latest): installs that follow 1.24 get the fix.

Plugins are versioned on their own (version in plugin.yaml, MAJOR.MINOR) and released from their own repositories; a plugin fix never waits for labdex.

docs.title: Branches
docs.text:
Branch For Protected main the next minor version; always green yes: pull requests with green CI only release/X.Y X.Y.0 and everything after it (X.Y.1, X.Y.0-1 …) yes: pull requests only feature/<topic>, fix/<topic> one change; short-lived no dependabot/… dependency updates, weekly no

Every change reaches main and release/* through a pull request. Pushes run the quick lint; pull requests run CI for what they touch: the backend tests on SQLite (only the tests the change affects), browser tests, the performance budget, the image and the docs. The tests also run on PostgreSQL when a change touches database code (models, migrations, queries, the driver), for every pull request into a release/* branch, when CI is run by hand, and every Monday on main.

docs.title: Making a release
docs.text:
1. Cut the branch when main has what the release should have: git switch -c release/1.24 main, then python backend/tools/bump.py minor (writes 1.24.0 everywhere and opens its CHANGELOG heading), fill in the CHANGELOG, and open a pull request into release/1.24. Nothing new goes in from here on: fixes only.
  2. Plugins first. If the release needs new plugin versions, merge and release those in their repositories (they're then in the Marketplace) and point the submodules at them in the same pull request.
  3. Release. When CI is green and the pull request is merged, publish a GitHub release on release/1.24 tagged v1.24.0 (gh release create v1.24.0 --target release/1.24 --notes ""). The release workflow checks the tag against the code, builds the image on amd64 and arm64, signs everything, attaches the files and the CHANGELOG section, and publishes this version's docs.
  4. Back to main. Merge release/1.24 into main (a pull request), so the version, the CHANGELOG and any fixes made on the branch are there too. Then bump.py minor on main starts 1.25.0.

docs.title: Fixing a release
docs.text:
1. Branch from the release branch: git switch -c fix/<topic> release/1.24.
  2. Fix it, with a test. python backend/tools/bump.py patch (1.24.0 → 1.24.0-1) and a CHANGELOG entry.
  3. Pull request into release/1.24; once merged, publish v1.24.0-1 on release/1.24.
  4. Pull request release/1.24 → main (or cherry-pick the fix), so the next version has it.

Only the newest release branch gets hotfixes, unless a fix is about security: then the previous one too.

docs.title: What each release has
docs.text:
• a GitHub release with the CHANGELOG section, the source (with the plugins), the wheel, their SBOMs and cosign bundles
  • ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:<version> for amd64 and arm64, signed, with its SBOM attached
  • its own docs: https://labdex-app.github.io/labdex/<X.Y>/ (the version picker at the top); latest is the newest release, dev is main

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] CHANGELOG: what changed, for the people running it (not the commits)
  • [ ] Upgrading from the previous release works (tests/test_upgrade_gate.py and the migration tests)
  • [ ] Docs describe the new behaviour; screenshots are current (docs/screenshots.py)
  • [ ] New plugin versions are released and the submodules point at them
  • [ ] CI is green on the pull request

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Everything is set with environment variables; conventions (domain, alias length, categories, the DMZ area) are edited in the UI under Settings → Conventions.

Variable Default LABDEX_DATA ./data (/data in the image) Database, secret.key, plugins/, backups LABDEX_DB sqlite:///$LABDEX_DATA/labdex.db or postgresql://user:pw@host/db LABDEX_SECRET_KEY generated into $LABDEX_DATA/secret.key Signs sessions, encrypts secrets. Keep a copy apart from backups LABDEX_ADMIN_USER, LABDEX_ADMIN_PASSWORD Create this administrator on an empty database LABDEX_PLUGIN_DIR $LABDEX_DATA/plugins Installed plugins LABDEX_PLUGIN_SANDBOX on Community and unsigned plugins run isolated (see Installing plugins). strict: only where the kernel has Landlock; off: inside labdex like official plugins LABDEX_SSO_HEADER e.g. Remote-User, trusted only from LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES LABDEX_SSO_GROUPS_HEADER e.g. Remote-Groups, matched to labdex groups by name LABDEX_SSO_AUTOCREATE false Create users on their first SSO visit LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES Proxy addresses allowed to send SSO headers LABDEX_OIDC_ISSUER Sign in with OpenID Connect, see below LABDEX_COOKIE_SECURE false true behind HTTPS LABDEX_SESSION_HOURS 12 Session lifetime LABDEX_SCHEDULER true Run scheduled actions and templates LABDEX_WORKER inline external: only queue jobs for labdex worker LABDEX_DEMO false Demo mode. Wipes the database: never on a real instance LABDEX_DEV_PLUGINS Development only: a folder of plugin checkouts (the repository's plugins/) loaded as official plugins. Never on a real instance

docs.title: Single sign-on with OpenID Connect
docs.text:
labdex signs people in with Authentik, Keycloak, Authelia, Pocket ID, Zitadel or any other OpenID Connect provider (authorization code flow with PKCE). Create an application there with the redirect URI https://<labdex>/api/auth/oidc/callback (Settings › Users shows the exact one), then:

Variable Default LABDEX_OIDC_ISSUER The issuer URL, e.g. https://auth.example.net/application/o/labdex/ LABDEX_OIDC_CLIENT_ID LABDEX_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET Empty for a public client (PKCE alone) LABDEX_OIDC_NAME single sign-on The button: "Sign in with Authentik" LABDEX_OIDC_SCOPES openid profile email groups LABDEX_OIDC_USERNAME_CLAIM preferred_username The labdex user name (else the email's local part) LABDEX_OIDC_GROUPS_CLAIM groups Matched to labdex groups by name (Keycloak's /a/b paths too) LABDEX_OIDC_ADMIN_GROUPS Comma separated: members are administrators (and only they) LABDEX_OIDC_AUTOCREATE true A first sign-in creates the account LABDEX_OIDC_ONLY false Hide the password form (setting up the first administrator still works)

An account is linked to the provider's subject at its first sign-in: an existing local account with the same user name is taken over once, after that a rename at the provider changes nothing. Group memberships follow the provider at every sign-in. Set the public URL (Settings › General) when labdex sits behind a proxy, so the redirect URI is right.

docs.title: SQLite or PostgreSQL
docs.text:
SQLite is right for almost every homelab. For PostgreSQL install the postgres extra (the image has it) and move an existing instance over:

labdex db copy --to postgresql://labdex:pw@db/labdex   # then set LABDEX_DB and restart
labdex db current                                     # schema revision

The schema is migrated on start; see Upgrading.

docs.title: Demo mode
docs.text:
LABDEX_DEMO=1 turns an instance into a public playground.

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -e LABDEX_DEMO=1 ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:1
  • On an empty database, and every night at 03:00 UTC, everything is wiped and the sample lab is loaded: networks, hosts, services, aliases and a zone policy (examples/homelab.yaml).
  • Sign in as demo / demo-labdex; the sign-in page says so, and a banner says when the next reset is.
  • The built-in Demo lab plugin (only there in demo mode) is a pretend DNS server and monitor: plan a DNS sync, approve it, watch it apply; one host has a bad day; the dashboard and host pages get widgets.
  • Nothing reaches a network. Only Demo lab and File exports can have instances; plugins can't make HTTP requests or run Ansible; installing plugins, repositories, notification channels, secrets, restores and changes to users and passwords are off.

Danger

Demo mode deletes everything in its database every night. Point it at its own data folder.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
labdex derives every record from the inventory:

  • A/AAAA per interface: <host>.<network>.<domain>, or into the network's own zone.
  • The host's short name, fun names and service names as CNAMEs in the domain (or the host's main zone).
  • SRV/TXT per service when DNS-SD is ticked.
  • Extra records per host (an alias that follows the primary record, A/AAAA, TXT, SRV, MX) and global custom records with {ip4}/{fqdn} placeholders.

Download them as a zone file or JSON (File exports), or let the Technitium plugin keep a server in step: it syncs every zone labdex uses, puts each record into the closest zone on the server, and only touches records it created.

docs.title: Split horizon
docs.text: A public service's name (dns.example.com) is served by your public DNS with your WAN address. With split horizon on, Technitium gets a zone of that name holding the service's internal addresses, so inside the house the name resolves straight to the host. labdex creates the zone as part of the plan and leaves public DNS alone.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
1. Zones. Under Zones create your areas (DC datacenter, CA campus, …); each gets a default zone. Add the zones you need inside them (DC_TC, CA_UT) with a rank and colour. "Load the example set" gives you a complete set to edit.
  2. Naming. Under Naming, check the categories and types for hostnames (<category>-<type>-<role>-<nn>) and pick or paste fun name pools.
  3. Networks. Add your VLANs with prefixes, gateways and DHCP ranges; each network sits in a zone.
  4. Hosts. Add hosts with interfaces (the next free address is suggested) and services (port, protocol, link, who may reach them).
  5. Lint. The Lint page tells you what breaks your conventions.
  6. Policy. Fill in the zone matrix: which zone may reach which, on which ports.
  7. Plugins. Add an instance of OPNsense, Technitium and others under Plugins, then run their actions. Changes come as plans you review on the Dashboard.

Or import a whole inventory at once: labdex import inventory.yaml (the format is what labdex export writes; examples/homelab.yaml is a complete example).

docs.title: Install
docs.text: labdex is one container (or one Python package) with a SQLite database in its data folder. PostgreSQL is optional.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker run -d --name labdex -p 8080:8080 -v labdex-data:/data \
  -e LABDEX_COOKIE_SECURE=true ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:1

Open http://127.0.0.1:8080. On an empty database the first visit asks you to create the administrator (or set LABDEX_ADMIN_USER and LABDEX_ADMIN_PASSWORD).

The image runs as an unprivileged user with a read-only root filesystem; only /data is written. Put labdex behind your reverse proxy over HTTPS.

Verify the image

Release images are signed with cosign (keyless, GitHub Actions OIDC) and carry an SBOM. See Security.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
The repository's docker-compose.yml starts labdex, and with --profile postgres a PostgreSQL next to it. A commented worker service runs jobs in their own container (Jobs and the worker).

git clone https://github.com/labdex-app/labdex && cd labdex
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec labdex labdex import --yes /app/examples/homelab.yaml   # optional sample data

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text:
cd frontend && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..   # builds the UI into backend/labdex/static
cd backend && pip install -e ".[server]"          # optional: ".[postgres,uptimekuma]", nmap, ansible-core
labdex user create admin --admin
gunicorn --workers 1 --threads 16 -b 127.0.0.1:8080 "labdex:create_app()"

Python 3.11 or newer. nmap is needed for the nmap plugin, ansible-core for the Ansible runner and the login banner plugin.

docs.title: Networks
docs.text: A network has a name, VLAN, zone, IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes (several are fine), a gateway and a DHCP range. labdex suggests the next free address (skipping the gateway and the DHCP pool), shows what's used, and lint checks that the third octet matches the VLAN if you want that convention. A network can name its own DNS zone.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
A host has a functional name, fun names, a kind (machine, VM, container, VIP), a status (active, planned, offline, legacy), the hypervisor it runs on, tags, features, variables, a vendor, model and icon, and interfaces. Each interface has a name and type, sits in a network with IPv4/IPv6 addresses (plus secondary addresses) and a MAC; one is primary. An interface can sit on another one (a VLAN on a bond, a VM's NIC on its hypervisor's bridge srv-pm-pve-01:vmbr0). Cables connect a port on one host to a port on another (switch ports needn't be interfaces); a port holds one cable. An internal link joins a guest's interface to a bridge of the host it runs on (or two guests of one host); a bridge holds as many as you like. A VIP is a host whose members are other hosts; VIPs have their own tab on the Hosts page, next to Physical and Virtual (a host that runs on another one, or a VM or container by the type in its name).

Addresses per family. An interface's addresses are edited like a network's prefixes: under IPv4 the main address and any more; under IPv6 an interface ID (used in every IPv6 prefix of the network) or an explicit address, and any more. The main ones are in DNS and used for monitoring; the others count for firewall aliases, IPAM and Discovery.

A host's dashboard. An existing host opens on Dashboard: its status and what monitors say, its addresses, where it sits (zone, hypervisor, guests, cables), links to its services, and what plugins show for it. The form is under Overview.

Addresses that last. Hosts, networks and zones have a short id that never changes (/hosts/7k2m9x4qa1): a link keeps working after a rename. Links by name (/hosts/srv-vm-dns-01) still work and move on to the id. A zone's page (/zones/<id>, from the code on the Zones page) lists its networks, the hosts at home there and what the zone policy lets in and out.

docs.title: Racks
docs.text: Inventory › Racks draws every rack as an elevation, front and rear side by side, unit 1 at the bottom, grouped by site (a room, a building). Click a free unit to put a host there (its height comes from the host's Size, in units (U, HE), set on its Overview), or a panel: a patch panel, cable management, a blank panel, a shelf, a PDU, with a label and a description ("24 × Cat6 to the office"). Each sits on the front, the rear or through the full depth. A host's ⋯ moves it or takes it out; a panel opens its settings. Two devices can share a unit on opposite sides; a full-depth one takes both. A host's Overview has the same fields, and its Dashboard says where it sits. People who edit hosts change racks; everyone else sees them, and only the hosts they may see.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
Network › Topology draws the lab two ways.

Physical. A host that others run on is a box with its guests inside, and its own interfaces as small ports, joined the way they're stacked (vmbr0 on bond0 on eno1 and eno2). Cables are solid lines in the cable's own colour (or coloured by speed: switch it on the legend) and thicker when faster, with the port names as small tags near their ends; a cable between two ports of one host is a loop. Internal links are dashed lines from a guest to the bridge it sits on. A guest whose interface doesn't say what it sits on is joined to its hypervisor's bridge in the same network, drawn fainter: a guess until you set it. VIPs aren't drawn here (they're addresses, not boxes with cables).

Networks (L3 / VLANs). Networks are nodes and every host is joined to the networks it has an address in; hosts in several networks are diamonds. A VIP is joined to the hosts that hold it. The chips above the map hide and show single networks (kept in your browser).

Hosts show their hostname below them and their fun name above, in their zone's colour or a colour of their own (Overview › Colour on the map). The fun name is a label of its own: drag it wherever it reads best and it stays there, following the host. Point at a host for a summary; click it for its links; click a line for its two ends and, for a cable, its medium, speed and notes, which people who edit hosts can change or remove right there. Cable draws a new one: click both ends (the same host twice for a cable between two of its ports).

The arrangement is shared: drag things where they belong and everyone sees the same map (people who edit hosts move it; Arrange again lays it out anew). Grid shows a dot grid and snaps what you drop to it.

Saved views keep a way of looking at it: the picture, the zone, hidden networks, the options and where you've zoomed to ("Rack room", "Kube networks"). Everyone who sees the topology can open them from the list or by link (/topology?v=<id>); people who edit hosts save, update and delete them. PNG and SVG download the whole picture.

docs.title: Cables
docs.text:
Inventory › Cables lists every cable you may see both ends of: its label (what's printed on it), both ends, medium, speed, length in metres and jacket colour. Next free continues the labels the lab already uses (C-0042 → C-0043); a label belongs to one cable only. Print labels prints a sheet with two labels per cable, one for each end, each naming this end and the other one (the ticked cables, or all shown). Label, length and colour are also on the cable dialogs of a host and of the topology.

Seen by switches. Switches that tell labdex their neighbours (the SNMP neighbours plugin reading LLDP and CDP, or UniFi signed in with a local account) feed the second tab of Cables. New lists cables between two known hosts that aren't on record: tick and Add them (each one goes through the host's normal checks and into History, a port the host doesn't have yet is added) or Ignore them for good. Different from the record lists ports where a switch sees something else than the cable on record: keep the record, or use what's seen (the old cable goes). Neighbours labdex doesn't know can become hosts with a click, prefilled with the address and MAC. A cable both ends report shows once; port names match whatever their case.

Patch panels. A patch panel is a host whose front ports pass straight through to its rear ports: on an interface, Passes through to names the port on the other side (set on one, both get it). Several adds a whole panel at once: tick Patch panel and every port gets a rear port (1 ↔ r1, 2 ↔ r2 …). Trace (on a host's port, a cable on the Cables page or a cable on the topology) follows a cable end to end through any number of panels: server eth0 → panel A 1 … r1 → panel B r3 … 3 → switch ge-0/0/5, with each cable's label, colour and length.

A host with four ports or more shows a front panel on its Dashboard and Network tab: its ports in order, odd ones on top, RJ45 and SFP-style cages apart, a cabled one in its speed's colour. Point at a port for where it goes; click it for its cable (or a new one).

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text: The Network tab lists physical interfaces (ethernet and Wi-Fi ports) first and virtual ones (bonds, bridges, VLANs, tunnels, loopbacks) below, each under what it sits on. A physical port has a connector (RJ45, SFP, SFP+, SFP28, QSFP+, QSFP28 …) and a speed; picking a connector offers its usual speed. Several adds many at once from a pattern: eth[0-3], 1/0/[1-48], swp[1-4]s[0-3] (every combination), Gi1/0/[01-24] (keeps the leading zero), with one type, connector, speed and network for all; names the host has already are skipped.

docs.title: Address map
docs.text: A network's Address map tab shows every address of its IPv4 prefix as a grid, a /24 at a time: in use, gateway, DHCP pool, seen (Discovery saw something there that no host has), conflict (two hosts have it, or Discovery saw a different MAC than the inventory has), free. Click a free address to make a host with it; click a seen one to add it as a host with what Discovery knows.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service has a name, port and protocol, a description, where it listens (every address, the primary interface, one network or one address), a link (https://…, by name or address; the DNS name may be relative to the host's zone, grafana, or a full name ending in a dot, grafana.example.com., which gets a record only inside a zone labdex writes), DNS-SD records if you tick them, and allow from: the zones, areas, networks or aliases that may reach it. That list drives the firewall access check and, with the OPNsense plugin, rules of its own.

A service can be public: it then gets a public name and a WAN port, a port forward on OPNsense and a split-horizon zone on Technitium (Zone policy).

The Services page is a launcher: every service with a link as a card, grouped by zone, with its status from a monitor or Discovery.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
nmap scans, the OPNsense ARP table, Kea leases, DNS records, Tailscale, UniFi clients and Proxmox guests the inventory doesn't have feed Discovery: unknown addresses, undocumented open ports, declared services that don't answer. One click adds a port to its host or an address to an existing host.

Where is …? (Discovery's last tab, or type a MAC or an address in the search with Ctrl K) finds the switch port behind any MAC, IP address or host: from the switches' forwarding tables, which the SNMP neighbours plugin reads (BRIDGE-MIB and Q-BRIDGE-MIB, per VLAN) and UniFi reports for its clients (wired: the switch port; Wi-Fi: the access point). A MAC shows on its own port and on every link between switches on the way; labdex pins the likely one (the fewest other MACs, not cabled to another switch). A host's Network tab shows that port next to each interface with a MAC and no cable on record.

A service is answering when a scan saw its port open on an address it listens on, and not answering only when a scan checked that port and found it closed. nmap checks the ports of every declared TCP service on its host, also ports outside its own list (a service on 32400 is looked at even with the top 200 ports), so a service is never reported down just because nobody looked; until then it shows not scanned.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text: Placement, duplicate IPs and MACs, octet vs. VLAN, alias length, unresolvable alias members, DNS name clashes, missing secrets, public services outside a DMZ and more. labdex lint exits non-zero on errors, so it can gate CI on your inventory YAML.

docs.title: Plans and approvals
docs.text:
Anything that changes another system is a plan first: the plugin computes the changes (each with before and after) and stops. You review it on the job page or the Dashboard and approve or discard it.

The job page groups the changes by kind. An update shows only the fields that change, before and after. While you may still approve, you can untick changes you don't want: the approval applies the rest, the job log says who left out what, and the plan keeps them marked. (An Ansible run is one change and can't be applied in part.)

  • A plan goes stale when the inventory changes before it's applied; it is planned again when it's approved. If the new plan has the same changes, approvals carry over.
  • A newer plan for the same action replaces the older one (approvals carry over the same way).
  • Hooks re-plan after inventory changes; schedules and job templates plan on a timer. All of them still wait for review.

docs.title: Approval policies
docs.text:
Settings → Approvals & windows. Policies are matched top to bottom by integration name, the zones of the hosts a plan touches and how it was started (by someone, a hook, a schedule). A policy sets:

approvals how many are needed; 0 applies by itself approvers users and @groups; empty = anyone who may apply the integration self approval whether whoever started the plan may approve it delay applies no sooner than this after planning window a change window it must wait for

Without a matching policy you approve your own plans.

docs.title: Change windows
docs.text:
Weekly times in a time zone, e.g. Tue and Thu 20:00–22:00 Europe/Zurich (a window may run past midnight). An approved plan waits as approved until its delay has passed and its window is open; the worker applies it then.

On the command line labdex action <integration> <action> --apply applies at once.

docs.title: The matrix
docs.text:
The Policy page is a matrix of zones: rows are where traffic comes from, columns where it goes. A cell holds ports and a reason:

  • any, a port alias (SG_WEB), or tcp/443, udp/53, tcp/8000-8100.
  • No cell means no access: anything not listed is denied.

Everyone can read the matrix; admins edit it. Changes are recorded in History, emit policy.updated, and are part of the YAML (zone_policy).

docs.title: Rules on OPNsense
docs.text:
The OPNsense plugin's Sync policy rules turns the matrix into pass rules:

  • one rule per cell and port entry, on the source zone's interfaces, from the source zone's alias to the destination zone's alias;
  • one rule per service allow from that the matrix doesn't already cover;
  • one rule per host-wide rule and port (a host's own allow from / allow to);
  • all of them in the category automation:labdex, keyed in the description ([zone:CA_ST>DC_TC:SG_WEB]).

Your own rules are never changed. Rules no policy explains lists your pass rules between zones the matrix doesn't allow, so you can move them into the matrix or remove them.

docs.title: Public services
docs.text: Tick public on a service, give it a public name and a WAN port. Sync port forwards plans a destination NAT rule per public service (WAN address and port to the host's address and the service's port), also in automation:labdex. Lint warns when a public service lives outside a DMZ zone.

docs.title: When is a zone done?
docs.text: Network › Policy › On the firewalls shows every firewall that enforces the matrix, with Sync policy rules next to each (a plan you review). Each has a Zones table: per zone, the labdex rules and the other pass rules on its interfaces, and gaps in the access check (declared access without a pass rule). A zone whose inbound pass rules all come from labdex and which has no gaps is managed by labdex. Check access logs those zones too.

docs.title: Users, roles, history
docs.text:
• Sign-in: local passwords (10+ characters, throttled after 5 failures), SSO headers from a trusted proxy, or API tokens (Authorization: Bearer ldx_…, optionally read-only and expiring, stored hashed).
  • Permissions are <type>:<action>: types host, network, alias, integration, discovery, audit, secret; actions view, edit, apply, admin. Built-in roles: viewer, editor, operator, integration-admin, secret-keeper, admin. For secrets a * (all actions) covers only view: revealing and changing them is always given by name (secret:apply, secret:edit). See the vault.
  • Role bindings give a user or group a role on a scope: *, zone:DC_*, area:CA, network:srv, tag:admin, name:srv-vm-*. An editor on zone:CA_* can't see or touch the datacenter.
  • Object grants add exceptions for single objects, e.g. edit on host:srv-vm-media-* or apply on integration:motd.
  • Moving an object needs edit rights on its old and its new place.
  • History records every create, update, delete, import, approval, apply and sign-in with a field diff. Hosts, networks and aliases can be reverted; a revert is a change of its own.

docs.title: The vault
docs.text: Root passwords, IPMI logins, Wi-Fi keys, recovery codes: the vault keeps them in labdex, next to the hosts they belong to, encrypted with a passphrase only you know.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
Inventory › Vault › Set up the vault (administrators). Choose a passphrase of at least 12 characters; a few words are easy to remember and hard to guess.

There is no way back from a lost passphrase. Neither labdex nor a backup can open the secrets without it. Write it down and keep it somewhere safe, apart from the backups.

docs.title: Sealed and unsealed
docs.text:
After every start of labdex the vault is sealed: names, paths and field names show, values don't. An administrator opens it on the Vault page with the passphrase; it stays unsealed until labdex stops or someone presses Seal. Five wrong passphrases in a minute and labdex waits a minute before it tries again; every attempt is in History.

While sealed, path, host and description of an entry can still change, values can't.

docs.title: Entries
docs.text:
An entry has a path (hosts/srv-pm-pve-01/root, wifi/iot: lowercase, up to 8 parts), an optional host, a description and its fields (username, password, url … up to 40). The ↻ button next to a value makes a 24-character password in your browser.

  • An entry of a host shows on the host's Secrets tab, and the host's rights apply to it (its zone, network, tags, name). Renaming the host keeps the link, and so does a YAML import.
  • Every change makes a new version; the last 10 are kept, and each can be revealed.
  • Values never appear in lists, exports, History or the API answers that list entries. The YAML export doesn't contain the vault; back it up with labdex's own backups.

docs.title: Revealing
docs.text: The eye shows one field, for 30 seconds; the copy button copies it without showing it. Both need secret:apply on the entry, and both are written to History (revealed hosts/srv-pm-pve-01/root#password). In the browser, labdex asks for your password again before the first reveal, and again after 5 minutes.

docs.title: Rights
docs.text:
Permission Lets you secret:view see paths, field names, versions (the viewer role has it) secret:apply reveal and copy values secret:edit add, change and delete entries

secret:apply and secret:edit are only ever given by name: a role with * (or secret:*) gets view only. The built-in secret-keeper role has both; bind it on a scope like zone:DC_* or name:wifi/* (path scopes work for entries without a host). Administrators may do everything and alone set up, unseal, seal and change the passphrase.

docs.title: Pointing at secrets
docs.text:
Plugins and Ansible variables don't hold a copy, they point at a field:

  • a plugin's secret setting: from the vault, then pick fw/opnsense#key;
  • an Ansible variable: api_key: {$secret: vault:fw/opnsense#key}.

The value is read when the job runs, so a changed secret reaches every user on its next run. Pointing at a secret for the first time needs secret:apply on it, because it hands the secret to the plugin or to Ansible; what someone else pointed at stays when you edit. An entry's dialog shows who uses it; it can't be deleted while anything does, and renaming it takes the references along.

While the vault is sealed, jobs that need a secret fail and say so. They run in the labdex process (the default); the separate labdex worker process can't read the vault.

Before 1.18 shared secrets lived under Settings › Secrets, encrypted with secret.key. They move into the vault as global/<name> (field value) the first time an administrator sets it up or unseals it, and {$secret: name} keeps meaning vault:global/<name>#value, so nothing that points at them breaks. /api/secrets still works on those global/ entries.

docs.title: How it's built
docs.text:
passphrase ──scrypt──▶ key-encryption key ──AES-GCM──▶ master key (random, 32 bytes)
master key ──AES-GCM──▶ a data key per version ──AES-GCM──▶ the values (JSON)
  • Only the wrapped master key is stored. The unwrapped one lives in the memory of the labdex process, never on disk.
  • Each ciphertext is bound to its entry and version, so blobs swapped between entries don't decrypt.
  • Changing the passphrase re-wraps the master key; the entries stay as they are.
  • secret.key (for integration settings) has nothing to do with the vault: neither opens the other.
  • labdex runs as one process (the Docker image starts one worker with threads). If you run several workers or processes, each one would have to be unsealed on its own; the separate labdex worker process never reads the vault.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
The start page is the shared Overview dashboard: cards on a grid. Edit (for administrators on shared dashboards, for you on your own) lets you drag a card by its handle, resize it from the corner, remove it, and add cards: the numbers, approvals, failing and running jobs, the last changes, what's coming up, hosts per zone, every plugin widget or just one, links of your own, the inventory's services with their status (all, or by tag, zone or category), and notes. Done saves; Cancel forgets. With a card's handle focused, the arrow keys move it and Shift + arrows resize it.

+ Dashboard makes another one: a page of links (a start page like Homarr's, built in), a wall for the rack room. Yours are only yours; administrators can make shared ones. Links open http(s) addresses or labdex pages, nothing else.

docs.title: Search and go
docs.text:
Ctrl K (⌘ K on a Mac), or / anywhere outside a text field, opens one search box for everything:

  • Hosts by name, fun name, function, tag, address or MAC. A MAC can be typed any way: AA-BB-CC-11-22-33, aabb.cc11.2233 or just aa:bb:cc.
  • Networks by name, by VLAN (vlan 100), or by an address inside them: type 10.10.100.53 and the network it belongs to shows up too.
  • Services, aliases (by name or firewall id) and integrations.
  • Actions of integrations you may run, like Check drift or Sync aliases: Enter starts it and opens the job.

  • Pages and New host / New VIP / New network.

  • Tags: tag:backup (or just a word that is a tag) offers the hosts list filtered to it.

↑ ↓ choose, Enter opens, Esc closes. You only find what you're allowed to see.

docs.title: Physical, virtual, tags
docs.text:
The Hosts page has three tabs: Physical (machines and appliances), Virtual (anything that runs on another host, plus VMs and containers by their name) and VIPs. Host on the Virtual tab starts a guest.

The search box on the hosts list takes plain words and terms, combined:

Term Matches tag:backup hosts tagged backup; several tag: terms must all match zone:dmz, status:offline, cat:srv zone, status, category on:srv-pm-pve-01 guests of that host net:srv hosts with an address in that network

Values with spaces go in quotes: tag:"off site". A tag chip in the list adds its term. Group by (tag, zone, runs on, category or status) puts a heading over each group; a host with two tags shows under both. Only these narrows the list to one group.

docs.title: Many hosts at once
docs.text:
On the hosts list, tick the hosts (Shift-click ticks a range; the box in the header ticks every host the filters show). The bar that appears offers:

  • Change: status, runs on, tags to add or remove, and an integration turned on or off for these hosts. Only what you set changes.
  • Delete, after a confirmation.

A change applies to all of them or to none: if one host doesn't accept it, nothing changes and the dialog says which host and why. Each host gets its own history entry (so each can be reverted), all with the same summary.

docs.title: Keeping your place
docs.text:
• Back from a host returns to the list where you left it: same scroll position, filters and search. Lists show what they had at once and refresh in the background.
  • Ctrl S (⌘ S) saves the host or network you're editing.
  • Leaving a host or network with unsaved changes asks first, also when closing the tab.
  • What you type in a host or network form is kept as a draft in this browser (for two weeks). Come back and the page offers it: Restore them or Discard. Nothing is applied until you press Save, and saving clears the draft.

docs.title: The topology map
docs.text:
Two views: Physical (hypervisors as boxes with their guests, cables between ports) and Networks (L3 / VLANs) (every network as a node, each host joined to the networks it has an address in; hosts in several networks, like routers and firewalls, are diamonds). Hosts show their icon. Cables are coloured by speed (1G blue, 2.5–5G cyan, 10G green, 25G amber, 40G and more red; grey below 1G or without a speed) and drawn thicker when faster; the legend shows the speeds on the map.

Drawing a cable: Cable, then click both ends (a host, or a port inside a hypervisor's box). The dialog offers each host's interfaces; an unnamed one can be named there, and New port… adds an interface to that host. The cable is saved on both hosts, with history. In the side panel of a host, the bin next to a cable removes it.

Everybody sees the same map, per view. People who may edit hosts arrange it: a node dragged somewhere stays there for everyone, and the hint says who moved it last. Arrange again starts over (after asking). People who only view can drag nodes for a moment, but the map goes back when they reload.

docs.title: The sidebar
docs.text: One section is open at a time: going to a page opens its section and closes the others, and a page under a list (a host) marks the list (Hosts). Collapse at the bottom, or Ctrl B, shrinks the sidebar to icons and back. Pages that plugins add live as tabs on their integration (Automation → Plugins → the integration), not in the sidebar.

docs.title: Light or dark
docs.text: The menu under your name has Theme: Auto (follows your system), Light or Dark. It's kept in this browser. The search box knows it too: type light or dark.

docs.title: Keyboard and phone
docs.text:
• Every list row that opens something can be reached with Tab and opened with Enter; "Skip to the page" (the first Tab) jumps past the sidebar.
  • In a dialog, Tab stays inside it and Esc closes it.
  • On a phone the sidebar is behind the menu button and the search button sits next to it; the hosts list keeps name, function, zone and status, and no page scrolls sideways.

docs.title: Zones
docs.text:
• An area says where something is: INET internet, CA campus, RA remote access, DC datacenter, DMZ perimeter. Areas are yours to define, each with a colour.
  • Every area has a default zone with the area's own code (DC): for networks, hosts and interfaces you haven't classified further. It shows as just the area.
  • Further zones are made one by one inside an area, <AREA>_<NAME>: DC_TC for trusted servers, DC_HT for management, CA_UT for IoT and guests. Each has a name, a rank (higher = more trusted) and optionally its own colour.
  • Codes are typed as names: Trusted clients becomes DC_TRUSTED_CLIENTS (capitals, spaces and dashes turn into _). An area's code is up to 16 letters or digits without _, since _ separates the area from the zone; a whole zone code is up to 48 characters. Short codes are still handy: they appear in prompts and firewall aliases (long alias names get a shortened firewall id).

Zones live on the interface: every address takes its network's zone. A host's home zone follows its primary interface unless you pin it; it decides RBAC scopes, the prompt colour and the placement check. A firewall sits in every zone it has an interface in; give it the zone of its management interface as home zone.

Lint enforces placement: a device never sits in a network ranked above its own zone. A CA_UT IoT device in a DC_TC server network is a warning. Zones without a rank (the area defaults) aren't checked.

docs.title: Hostnames
docs.text:
Functional names are <category>-<type>-<role>-<nn>, e.g. srv-vm-dns-01: categories and types come from the lists under Naming, the role is free text, and the number is the next free one. They say what a host does, which is what you want in a prompt, a firewall rule or a log line.

Fun names are what you remember (arcanine, resolver). A host can have several; each becomes a DNS CNAME and the first shows in the login banner and prompt. Pools of fun names ship with labdex; paste your own and tie them to a category or zone, and labdex suggests unused ones.

docs.title: Firewall aliases
docs.text:
labdex generates aliases per network, zone, area and host, and you add your own groups whose members reference hosts, networks, zones or other aliases:

Alias Holds N4_ZONE_DC_TC_SRV the IPv4 prefix of network srv NG_ZONE_DC_TC every network in zone DC_TC NG_ZONE_DC every network in area DC NG_ZONE_DC_DEFAULT the networks in DC's default zone H_ZONE_DC_TC_SRV_VM_DNS_01 the addresses of one host HG_…, MG_…, SG_… your host, MAC and port groups

On the firewall each alias gets a short uid (ldx_3fa9c201, stable for its name) or, if you prefer under Settings → Conventions, a readable id (the name if it fits, else a shortened form); you can also set one per custom alias. The full name goes into the description. The OPNsense plugin can import the aliases you already have on the firewall.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
The backup module exists from the first start and backs up daily to /data/backups. Each backup holds a database snapshot and the inventory YAML as .tar.gz, encrypted with your passphrase (scrypt and AES-256-GCM). Targets: a folder (local or NFS) or S3 (AWS, MinIO, Garage); S3 needs a passphrase. Retention is a number of backups.

Keep secret.key somewhere else (password manager, offline): without it the secrets in a backup can't be decrypted, and a backup without its passphrase is useless.

labdex backup check labdex-backup-20261023-020000.tar.gz.enc
labdex backup restore FILE --inventory-only       # just the inventory, the server may run
labdex backup restore FILE                        # the whole database: stop the server first

Every backup carries a portable database.json, so it restores into SQLite or PostgreSQL alike.

docs.title: Jobs and the worker
docs.text:
Integration actions run as jobs from a queue in the database. A dispatcher claims a job, runs it and sends heartbeats; a job whose worker stops (no heartbeat for 90 seconds) is marked failed instead of hanging.

By default the web server runs jobs itself (LABDEX_WORKER=inline), which is all a single container needs. To keep long Ansible runs and scans out of the web process, or to run several gunicorn workers on PostgreSQL, set LABDEX_WORKER=external on the web server and start workers with the same database and data folder:

labdex worker --slots 2      # runs queued jobs, the scheduler and approved plans

About shows who runs jobs and how many wait; the Dashboard warns when nobody does. Job output streams live over Server-Sent Events. Each host has a Runs tab with the jobs that ran for it.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Channels under Settings → Notifications: ntfy (server, topic, token, priority), Matrix (homeserver, room, access token), email (SMTP with STARTTLS or SSL) and webhooks (JSON; with a secret, an X-Labdex-Signature: sha256=… HMAC of the body). Each channel picks its events and, optionally, the integrations it hears about.

Event When plan.waiting a plan needs approval plan.applied a plan was applied job.failed a job failed backup.failed a backup failed host.down, host.up a monitoring source changed a host's status policy.updated the zone matrix changed plugin.<id>.<event> anything a plugin sends with ctx.notify test the Test button

Messages go out from the worker through an outbox; failed ones are retried after 1, 5, 15 and 60 minutes. Set Address of this labdex (Settings → General) so messages link back to the job.

docs.title: Security review (1.0)
docs.text: Before 1.0 the parts of labdex that face users, plugins and files were reviewed again. This page records what was looked at, what changed, and what is left by design.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Looked at Result Password hashing scrypt with a per-user salt; a login for an unknown user costs the same as a real one Brute force Before: 5 failures per (address, user) in 5 minutes. Behind a reverse proxy every client had the proxy's address, so one person could lock a user out for everyone, and many addresses could try one user without limit. Fixed: the address is the client's (the last X-Forwarded-For hop that isn't a trusted proxy), and there is also a limit of 20 failures per user from anywhere. The table of failures can't grow without bound. Sessions HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Secure with LABDEX_COOKIE_SECURE; a password change ends every session (password version in the session) CSRF every write needs X-Requested-With: labdex, which no other site can send without a CORS preflight labdex never allows API tokens 256-bit random, stored as SHA-256, compared in constant time; optional read-only and expiry SSO headers only trusted from LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES; users are created only with LABDEX_SSO_AUTOCREATE Headers CSP without inline scripts, no framing, nosniff, same-origin referrer. Added: Permissions-Policy, Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy, and HSTS when cookies are secure.

docs.title: Server-Sent Events
docs.text: Looked at Result Who may watch a job checked when the stream opens (integration view right) A stream outliving its session Fixed: every 15 seconds the stream checks that the user is still active, the session's password unchanged and the API token still valid; otherwise it ends. Exhausting server threads Fixed: at most 8 open streams per user (429 beyond).

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Looked at Result Archive extraction absolute paths, .., drive letters and symlinks refused; entries count and size capped. Fixed: the size is now counted while unpacking, so a zip whose directory lies about sizes can't fill the disk. Before code runs manifest, labdex version range and signature are checked before any plugin code is imported; a plugin whose files changed after signing isn't loaded Repositories the key is pinned when added; index and plugins must be signed with it; downloads must match the index's SHA-256 Official plugins not part of the package (1.24.1+): installed from the official repository, signed with the project key, like any repository plugin What a plugin can do official and built-in plugins: anything labdex can. Community and unsigned plugins (1.5+) run in a process of their own with an empty environment, locked by Landlock to Python, their own folder, a data folder of their own and a private temporary folder; they get the plugin API over a pipe, with only their own instance's settings. Their Ansible playbooks run inside the same lock. labdex's own process is non-dumpable, so no plugin can read its memory. Unsigned plugins still need an administrator's explicit OK. Demo mode plugins can't make HTTP requests or run Ansible, only the demo plugins can have instances

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Looked at Result Encryption scrypt-derived key, AES-256-GCM, authenticated Restore archive entries must be plain files at the top level, and every file must match the manifest's SHA-256. Fixed: the unpacked size is capped, so a gzip bomb can't exhaust memory. Secrets encrypted with secret.key, which is never in a backup

docs.title: By design
docs.text:
• Administrators can make labdex connect to any address (integrations, notification channels, repositories). That is their job; don't give admin to people you wouldn't give network access.
  • Login throttling is per process. With several gunicorn workers, each counts on its own.
  • Anyone who can write to the data folder can add plugin code. Protect /data.
  • An isolated plugin still reads the whole inventory (as the plugin API offers) and can reach the network: it can send what it reads anywhere. Isolation keeps secrets and labdex itself safe, not the inventory's contents.
  • Without Landlock in the kernel (before Linux 5.13, or a container runtime that blocks it), on still runs isolated plugins in their own process, but they could read files labdex can. The Plugins page says which applies; strict refuses to run them then.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
• Put labdex behind a reverse proxy over HTTPS and set LABDEX_COOKIE_SECURE=true. SSO headers are only trusted from LABDEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES.
  • The container runs as an unprivileged user with a read-only root filesystem; only /data is writable.
  • Give every integration its own least-privilege API user or token.
  • Back up /data and keep secret.key apart from the backups.

docs.title: What labdex does
docs.text:
• Passwords are hashed with scrypt; sign-in is throttled after 5 failures per user and client address (the real client behind a trusted proxy) and 20 per user overall. API tokens are stored hashed and can be read-only and expiring.
  • Session cookies are HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict; every write needs the header X-Requested-With: labdex, so other sites can't post to labdex. A strict Content-Security-Policy, no framing.
  • Secrets are encrypted at rest (Fernet: AES with HMAC) and never returned by the API. They are masked in job logs.
  • The vault is sealed after every start: its master key is wrapped with a passphrase that labdex never stores (scrypt, AES-256-GCM, a key per version), so a backup or a copy of the database alone opens nothing. Every reveal is in History.
  • Every change is in History with who, when and what.
  • Plugins are checked (manifest, version range, signature) before any of their code runs; a plugin whose files no longer match its signature isn't loaded.
  • Backups are encrypted with your passphrase (scrypt, AES-256-GCM) and checked before a restore.

See the security review for what was checked before 1.0.

docs.title: Verifying a release
docs.text:
Release images and archives are signed with cosign, keyless, from the release workflow, and come with an SPDX SBOM:

cosign verify ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:1 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/labdex-app/labdex/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/v.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
cosign verify-blob labdex-1.0.0.tar.gz --bundle labdex-1.0.0.tar.gz.bundle \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/labdex-app/labdex/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Please report security problems privately through GitHub's Report a vulnerability on the repository, not in a public issue. What's supported, what happens after a report and what doesn't count: SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text: A template is an action with its parameters (and host, for host actions) saved under a name on the integration's page. Run it with one click, or on a schedule: every N minutes, or on chosen days at a time in a time zone. Scheduled plans go through approvals like any other. A schedule runs unattended, so it needs admin rights on the integration.

docs.title: Secrets in variables
docs.text:
Feature and host variables can point at a field of a vault entry:

vars:
  admin_password: {$secret: vault:apps/grafana#admin}
  db_password: {$secret: grafana-db}   # older form: vault:global/grafana-db#value

Pointing at a secret for the first time needs secret:apply on it (the right to reveal it); what someone else pointed at stays when you edit. A run needs the vault unsealed.

The value is filled in only while labdex runs Ansible (in a private temporary folder) and never reaches the inventory, the YAML export, the API or History. Secret values are masked as ******** in job logs, --diff included. Lint reports references to secrets that don't exist.

docs.title: Ansible Vault
docs.text:
• The Ansible runner takes a vault password (and optional vault id) for files in your playbooks encrypted with ansible-vault.
  • File exports: with a vault password, the Ansible inventory export writes secrets as !vault values, so playbook runs outside labdex decrypt them with the same password.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
1.24.1: the image has a new name

labdex moved to the GitHub organization labdex-app. From 1.24.1 on, the image is ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex; ghcr.io/reykimedev/labdex stays at 1.24.0 and gets no more updates. Change the image in your compose file (or docker run) once, then upgrade as below. Your data, settings and plugins stay as they are.

services:
  labdex:
    image: ghcr.io/labdex-app/labdex:1

Replace the image or package and start labdex: the database schema is migrated on start, from any release since 0.4. There are no manual steps, and the CI checks this by upgrading a 0.5 database to the current release.

docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
labdex db current       # the schema revision, if you're curious

Take a backup first (labdex backup create -o FILE) if you want a way back: a migrated database can't be opened by the older release.

docs.title: Within 1.x
docs.text:
From 1.0 on, labdex keeps within a major version:

  • the plugin API (see the reference): manifest keys, methods and their arguments only grow;
  • the REST API under /api: fields and endpoints are added, not removed or renamed;
  • the YAML format: older files import;
  • the backup format: older backups restore.

Anything else that has to go is deprecated in a minor release, noted in the changelog, and removed in the next major one.

Plugins say which versions they work with (labdex: ">=1.0,<2"); one outside its range after an upgrade isn't loaded, and its page says why.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
labdex itself has no plugins installed apart from backups, which are part of it. Every other plugin, the official ones too, comes from Plugins › Marketplace: installing one downloads it from its repository and checks its signature first. Uninstalling one is refused while it has instances.

Upgrading from 1.24.0 or older, where the official plugins shipped inside labdex: labdex installs the ones you had from the official Marketplace by itself, right after the upgrade. If it can't reach the Marketplace, the Plugins page lists them (with an Install them now button); their instances keep their settings and history meanwhile.

The Marketplace also lists what your repositories offer, with a filter for updates. Anyone who can see integrations can browse it; administrators install.

Under Plugins add an instance of a plugin (an integration), fill in its settings and enable it. A plugin can have several instances, e.g. one per firewall. Each plugin has a page listing its instances, what it can do and its signature.

Plugin What it does OPNsense Aliases, rules from the zone matrix, port forwards, Kea reservations, access check, ARP and leases into Discovery Technitium DNS Records and split-horizon zones, plan/apply; stale and unmanaged records per host Ansible runner Features as playbooks and roles, --check --diff as the plan; host actions Login banner & prompt Banners and a zone-coloured prompt over Ansible nmap TCP connect scans of inventory networks into Discovery; every declared service port is checked too, whatever the port list VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus Host status from up, CPU and memory widgets Beszel Host status and resources; adds systems, installs agents Uptime Kuma A monitor per service; status read back Certificates TLS expiry of every https service Proxmox VE Imports guests as hosts, links, drift k3s / Kubernetes Nodes, readiness, versions, drift Tailscale / Headscale Tailnet devices into Discovery, online state UniFi Network Clients into Discovery, devices as host status, cables from LLDP SNMP neighbours Cables from LLDP and CDP over SNMP v2c/v3 Traefik HTTP routers as services with their host names Docker Containers as hosts, published ports and Traefik labels as services, state as status Routing discovery BGP neighbours and routes vs. the inventory (FRR, IOS-XE) Prometheus service discovery http_sd_configs endpoints Backup Daily encrypted backups to a folder or S3 (Backups) YAML mirror The inventory as a file after every change, optionally in git File exports OPNsense alias import, DNS zone, Ansible inventory, DHCP CSV, YAML

docs.title: Applies to
docs.text: Integrations that work per host have selectors in the same syntax as role scopes. On a host's page each one shows whether it applies (and why), can be forced on or off, holds the host's own settings and actions, and shows a panel the plugin fills.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: API keys and tokens typed into a plugin's settings are encrypted at rest with a key derived from secret.key and are never sent back by the API. Shared ones live in the vault: pick from the vault on a secret setting and choose a field (vault:fw/opnsense#key); rotating it there updates every user. The list holds what you may reveal, since pointing at a secret hands it to the plugin.

docs.title: Widgets and status
docs.text: Plugins can show widgets on the dashboard and host pages, and report host and service status. A host is down if any monitoring source says so, up if one says up; without monitoring, Discovery's last scan decides.

docs.title: Ansible and features
docs.text:
Features are a tree (server → server.packages → server.packages.pve) with variables and playbooks or roles. Hosts get features; variables merge root to leaf, then the host's own variables. Making kube.cluster.oak makes kube and kube.cluster too when they don't exist yet (empty, ready for their own variables), in the UI, the API and a YAML import.

features:
  - {path: server, vars: {ntp: 10.10.3.253, pkgs: [vim, curl]}}
  - {path: server.packages, playbooks: [playbooks/packages.yml]}
  - {path: kube, vars: {version: v1.30.6}, roles: [k3s]}
  - {path: kube.cluster.oak, vars: {version: v1.31.2, vip: 10.10.128.10}}
hosts:
  - name: srv-vm-k3s-01
    features: [server.packages, kube.cluster.oak]
    vars: {k3s_role: server}

The Ansible runner applies features from a folder or a git repository: playbooks, then roles, ancestors first, each limited to the hosts that have the feature. --check --diff is the plan, the real run happens on apply. Per host it can apply the host's features, run a command or install packages.

Variables can point at a secret instead of holding it: {$secret: grafana-admin}. The value is filled in only while Ansible runs and is masked in logs. Files encrypted with ansible-vault work with the vault password setting; see Templates and Ansible Vault.
