The same variables and feature_<path> groups are in the Ansible inventory export, so your own ansible-playbook runs see them too.

docs.title: Proxmox VE
docs.text:
A read-only API token (PVEAuditor) is enough for importing and drift. Import guests plans VMs and containers as hosts (names that don't follow your convention become srv-vm-<name>-NN with the guest name kept as fun name), links existing hosts, and reports drift (addresses, MACs, status) between the inventory and the cluster.

Check drift also hands the guests the inventory doesn't have to Discovery (turn Guests labdex doesn't know go into Discovery off to stop it): their addresses show up under unknown hosts as Proxmox VM 104 on pve1, with the guest name as host name and its MAC when it has one network card. Running guests count as seen; Add it as a host starts from there.

docs.title: Creating guests
docs.text:
Off until you turn on Create guests in the instance; the token then needs the PVEVMAdmin role plus Datastore.AllocateSpace on the storage and SDN.Use on the bridges. Then the inventory is where a guest starts:

  1. Add a host with status planned, an interface with its address in a network, and Runs on set to a Proxmox node (or set a default node in the instance). The type comes from the name (srv-ct-… is a container, srv-vm-… a VM) or from the host's Proxmox settings, where cores, memory, disk, storage and the template can be set per host too.
  2. Run Create planned guests (or Create this guest on the host). The plan shows each guest: node, template, size, bridge, VLAN tag and addresses. Nothing in Proxmox changes until the plan is approved.
  3. On apply, a container is made from the LXC template, a VM is cloned from the cloud-init template; the network comes from the inventory: the network's VLAN as the tag on the bridge (or the bridge per network you set), the static address with the network's gateway, IPv6 from the inventory or SLAAC, your SSH keys, DNS server and search domain. A MAC the inventory doesn't have yet is generated (Proxmox's BC:24:11 prefix) and written back, so DHCP reservations and drift line up.
  4. The host is linked to its guest and becomes active once started. If a later step fails (the VM doesn't start, say), the guest is still linked and the host set offline, so the next plan doesn't make a second one; the job log says what to fix.

Guests are never deleted or changed after creation; drift reports differences.

docs.title: k3s
docs.text: A service account token with get/list on nodes and pods. Matches nodes to hosts, reports Ready/NotReady as host status, lists drift against the cluster's feature and mixed kubelet versions.

docs.title: Tailscale
docs.text: Tailscale or Headscale. Tailnet devices go into Discovery; devices that are hosts report online as status. Widgets for the tailnet and a host's device.

docs.title: UniFi
docs.text:
Clients go into Discovery with address, MAC and name; UniFi devices (switches, access points, gateways) that are hosts report online or offline. Read-only. Sign in with:

Setup Choose You need UniFi OS Server (self-hosted), or a console (UDM, UCG, Cloud Key) Local account — UniFi OS Server or console the URL (https://host:11443 for UniFi OS Server, port 443 on a console), a local account The Network application installed on its own Local account — Network application the URL with port 8443, a local account A console with Network 9.3 or newer API key Network → Settings → Control Plane → Integrations Anything adopted in unifi.ui.com Site Manager API key unifi.ui.com → API → Create API key

The form only shows what the chosen sign-in needs.

The account. Make one for labdex: Admins & Users → add an admin, Restrict to local access only, role View Only for Network. Accounts with two-factor sign-in (UI.com accounts usually) can't be used; labdex says so. labdex signs out after each run.

Site Manager. labdex lists the consoles the key sees (or the ones named under Consoles) and reads each through the UniFi cloud connector, which needs a recent console firmware. A console the connector can't reach still reports its devices from Site Manager, without clients; the job log says which. The certificate of api.ui.com is always checked.

Cables. Signed in with a local account, Read devices also reads which port everything sits on: each switch's LLDP neighbours, each device's uplink, and the switch port of every wired client. They show up as suggestions under Inventory › Cables › Seen by switches. A wired client has no port name of its own; its interface with that MAC is used (and named eth0 if it has no name yet). The API key sign-ins don't tell ports.

TLS. UniFi uses a self-signed certificate. Either leave Check the TLS certificate off, or install a real certificate (or set a CA file) and turn it on.

docs.title: SNMP neighbours
docs.text:
Reads switches and routers over SNMP, v2c (a community) or v3 (a user with SHA, SHA-256, SHA-512 or MD5 authentication and AES-128 privacy): who sits on which port, from LLDP and, on Cisco gear, CDP. What it finds becomes suggested cables under Inventory › Cables › Seen by switches; it also reports whether each switch answers, and a host's Dashboard shows its neighbours.

It starts with the hosts tagged snmp; change Applies to for more. A host is asked at its primary address, or at the one its Address for SNMP says. Neighbours are matched to hosts by the name they announce (any name labdex knows, with or without the domain), the chassis MAC (an interface MAC in the inventory) or the management address. Ones labdex doesn't know are listed too, with a button to add them as hosts.

Give the community or the v3 passphrases from the vault to share them between instances. SNMPv3 passphrases need eight characters at least. Read-only: labdex never sets anything.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: OPNsense with FRR (its diagnostics API) or Cisco IOS-XE (RESTCONF). Lists BGP neighbours (matched to hosts), routed prefixes that aren't an inventory network, and inventory networks the router has no route for. A neighbour leaving Established notifies.

docs.title: Traefik
docs.text: Read-only, Traefik v2 or v3 API (api.insecure, or behind a router with basic auth). Import services from routers plans a service per HTTP router with a Host rule: on the host its backend points at, or, when the backend isn't in the inventory (a container address), on the Traefik host with port 443/80. The router's host name becomes the service's DNS name (grafana.example.com., a full name), so the Services page links to it. A Routers page shows each router, its backend and whether the inventory has it.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Read-only Engine API, best through a socket proxy that only allows containers and the version (e.g. CONTAINERS=1). Import containers plans:

  • a host per container (srv-ct-<service>-NN, the container name as fun name), running on the Docker host, in its zone; an interface only where the container has an address in an inventory network (macvlan/ipvlan);
  • services: published ports on the Docker host (that's where they listen), Traefik router labels as services with the router's host name on the container's host.

Turn off "containers as hosts" to get only services on the Docker host. Read container state reports running / stopped as host status.

docs.title: Installing plugins and trust
docs.text:
Plugins › Marketplace installs what the official repository and your own repositories offer; Settings › Plugins uploads a .zip and manages repositories and keys. For a download, labdex unpacks the archive, validates the manifest, checks the labdex version range and the signature before any plugin code runs, then shows what you're about to install.

Trust Means built in part of labdex and only updates with it (backups, the demo lab) official maintained by the labdex project in its own repository, signed with the project key, from the official repository community signed with the key of a repository you added, or an author key you trust unsigned no signature: installs only after you tick "I trust its author" invalid bad signature, unknown key or files changed after signing: never loaded

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text:
A repository is a signed index.json next to the plugin archives, on any web server. Its key signs the index and every plugin in it. When you add one, labdex shows its name and key id: compare it with the one the publisher gives you. The key is pinned from then on; a re-signed index or a plugin signed with another key is refused.

The official Marketplace (labdex-plugins) is trusted out of the box. Every official plugin lives in its own git repository; its signed releases are the versions you can install.

Every plugin labdex ships (OPNsense, Technitium, Proxmox, Ansible, Backup, …) is an official plugin: it works from the first start without a download, and a fix for one arrives through the official repository without waiting for a labdex release. An installed update takes the shipped copy's place; removing the update ("Remove update") goes back to the shipped one, and integrations keep running either way. A broken update never replaces a working copy.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text:
A plugin names the labdex versions it works with (labdex: ">=1.0,<2"). labdex refuses to install one outside its range, doesn't load an installed one that falls outside after an upgrade, and the Marketplace marks it as needing another labdex.

A plugin's details in the Marketplace show what's new since the version you have, and every version its repository offers, with its notes: install any of them, newer or older (each goes through the same signature check). Updates go to the newest version that isn't withdrawn and works with your labdex.

  • Switch back: after an update the version it replaced is kept, so you can go back to it in one step (and forward again the same way), even offline.
  • Stay on a version: a held plugin isn't offered updates and never updates by itself.
  • Withdrawn versions: a publisher can withdraw a version (a serious bug, say). If you have it, the Marketplace says so, with the reason, and offers a way off it; updates skip it.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
Settings › Plugins › Updates decides what happens when a repository has something new (labdex looks every six hours, or when you press Check now):

Setting Does Tell me (default) a notification for each new version, once (event plugins.update); nothing is installed Install official updates updates signed with the labdex project key install by themselves and land in History (plugins.updated, or plugins.update_failed); others are announced Off no checks, no notifications; the Marketplace still shows updates when you open it

An installed version that gets withdrawn is announced too (plugins.withdrawn). Route these events to ntfy, Matrix, email or a webhook under Settings › Notifications.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
Official and built-in plugins run inside labdex. Community and unsigned plugins run isolated: every call (an action, a page, a widget) starts a process of its own with an empty environment, which locks itself with Linux's Landlock before the plugin is loaded. It can read Python and the plugin's own folder and write to a data folder of its own (plugin-data/<instance>) and a temporary folder; nothing else. So it can't open labdex's database, secret.key, other plugins or other integrations' secrets, can't read labdex's memory and can't signal it. Its Ansible playbooks run inside the same lock, and secrets from the vault ({$secret: …}) aren't filled in for it.

What it gets is the plugin API: the inventory, its own instance's settings and host settings, state, host status, notifications, discovery records. It can still reach the network, so treat what the inventory holds as visible to it.

The Plugins page shows which plugins run isolated and whether this machine supports Landlock. Set LABDEX_PLUGIN_SANDBOX=strict to refuse isolated plugins where it doesn't, or off to run them inside labdex (as before 1.5).

Warning

Install plugins you trust. Isolation limits what a plugin can take; it doesn't make a plugin's own actions (the changes it plans) trustworthy.

docs.title: VictoriaMetrics / Prometheus
docs.text: Reads up from a VictoriaMetrics or Prometheus API: a host is down when every target that belongs to it is down. CPU and memory widgets on host pages.

docs.title: Beszel
docs.text: Host status, CPU, memory and disk from Beszel agents. Adds hosts as systems (plan/apply) and installs the agent over Ansible.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text: Plans a monitor per service that has a link and reads host and service status back. Needs the uptimekuma extra (in the image).

docs.title: Certificates
docs.text:
Checks the TLS certificate of every https service (and endpoints you list): days left, issuer, names; warns before expiry and notifies.

Status from any of these shows as live dots on Hosts and in the sidebar, on the Services page, and as host.down / host.up notifications.

docs.title: OPNsense
docs.text:
Checked against OPNsense 26.1. Give labdex its own API user with access to the pages for the actions you use: aliases, automation filter rules, destination NAT, Kea DHCP, interfaces and diagnostics (ARP).

Action Mode Check connection run Sync aliases plan generated and custom aliases, category automation:labdex; adds hosts to aliases you made by hand and only removes what it added Sync policy rules plan rules from the zone matrix and services' allow from Sync port forwards plan destination NAT for public services Sync DHCP reservations plan Kea DHCPv4 reservations from MAC/IP pairs Check access run every service's allow from against the pass rules Import ARP / leases run into Discovery

Pages: Firewall access (the access check for every host). How the firewall matches the zone matrix (pending rule changes, rules no policy explains, zones managed by labdex) is on Network › Policy › On the firewalls. On a host: the rules that mention it and its access check.

Settings worth knowing: wan_interface and nat_destination for port forwards.

Everything labdex writes carries the category automation:labdex and a key in the description; it never changes anything else.

docs.title: Technitium DNS
docs.text:
Checked against Technitium DNS Server 15.6. Use an API token limited to the zones labdex manages.

  • Sync records (plan): the inventory's records plus custom ones, into the closest zone on the server. Only records it created (marked in their comment) are changed or removed.
  • Split horizon (setting, on by default): each public service name becomes an internal zone with the service's internal addresses. The zone is created as part of the plan.
  • Per host: every record that belongs to it, flagged in sync, missing, stale or unmanaged.
  • Records pointing at addresses that aren't in the inventory go into Discovery.
